en: The Scripture on the Samādhi of Expounding the Great Way and Manifesting It Widely, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One;
also titled The Scripture on Entering the Diamond-like State of Concentrated Intent.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: Attaining the Mind of Universal Wisdom (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on the summit of Vulture Peak in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and eight thousand bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a vast assembly of hundreds of thousands of beings as he extensively expounded the Dharma.

Then there was a dragon king named Anavatapta (translated into Chinese as "Without Heat"), who had planted roots of virtue in past lives and followed the practice of the bodhisattvas, firmly abiding in the Mahāyāna. He practiced the six perfections and, possessing the marks of fulfillment, diligently saved sentient beings through the infinite path of transformation.

He has served ninety-six billion Buddhas, accumulating merits beyond measure. Wielding skillful means, he manifests universally throughout the five realms of existence to uproot the darkness of ignorance, leading all to cultivate the desireless practice of a Bodhisattva; cherishing the four immeasurable minds, he delivers all beings.
Out of compassion for those subject to retribution, he manifested as a dragon, transforming hundreds of millions of dragons and causing them to escape their karmic calamities.

He established himself by the pond, leading a retinue of eight hundred million followers and bringing along one hundred and forty thousand court ladies who surrounded him as attendants, performing various musical entertainments. Their voices were harmonious and elegant, moving like the dragon upon which they rode; endowed with majestic virtue and sovereign spiritual transformations, they carried diverse flowers and offered the most exquisite incense, holding up banners and canopies as they approached the World-Honored One.

Upon arrival, they immediately prostrated themselves and respectfully inquired after the Tathāgata. Then, taking with them incense, flowers, various jewels, silken fabrics, banners, and canopies, and having further adjusted their musical instruments with joyful hearts and reverent minds, they approached the Buddha together with their retinues and female attendants. They knelt before him, solemnly joining their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to question the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Equal and Most Perfectly Awakened One!"
"What should be the path that a bodhisattva ought to practice?
Only if I am granted permission may I venture to ask.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon King, saying:
"Ask whatever you wish, without hesitation or difficulty; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha shall expound and explain it according to your mind."
At that time, Anavatapta, having been granted permission by the Honored One to pose his questions, felt even greater joy in his heart and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Celestial Teacher is the most honored one, the sage guide among men. As majestic as a lion, he manifests immeasurable transformations.
I ask the Tathāgata for the sake of all sentient beings, and also for the sake of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, so that they may become teachers of the world."
He has transcended worldly dharmas; his will and conduct are pure, clearly exhausting all causes and conditions.
He delivers all living beings as an unasked friend, universally providing peace, rescue, guidance, and support.
Upholding fearlessness and the ten powers, he advances to subdue all māras and defeat all heterodox paths. His mind is free from defiled conduct, and he is clad in the firm adamantine armor.
The armor of the Great Virtuous One is such that his resolve never grows weary; the accumulation of the causes and conditions of merit is immeasurable.

Having fully perfected giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, his mind is equal toward all things, having eliminated all disparate characteristics and abandoned the two views.
Thus he transcends through the perfection of wisdom, understands the nature of dependent origination, and has entered the profound depths.
The essential point of the ultimate difficulty is to abandon the thoughts of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, not to forsake the mind of great vehicle omniscience,
to maintain firm and resolute mental conduct that is always sovereign, to have a body that is pure, stainless, radiant, and translucent,
and to have a will like space that does not weary throughout incalculable kalpas— one who acts thus attains dhāraṇī.
He eliminates greed, defilement, self-importance, and arrogance, becoming equal to one who has passed away;
through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he transcends all things as if they were a dream, an illusion, a reflection, an echo, a mirage, or the moon in water.
Regarding these dharmas, he attains a non-discriminating understanding and remains unmoved; he reveres and honors the teachings of the Triple Gem, turning the Wheel of Dharma without attachment.
Obstacles, as well as joy, delight, faith, and aspiration, are all spontaneously attained.

Like the udumbara flower, which appears but rarely in billions of eons, those whose will is tranquil and who dwell alone possess universal marks of excellence. Having long cultivated reverence and being wise great beings (*mahāsattva*), they honorably practice the supreme meaning; as the Dharma abides in this manner, it is for the sake of those true gentlemen that one questions the Tathāgata.

I only pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will explain the conduct of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, so that they may attain the Dharma-gate of wandering freely, enter the fruit of adamantine virtue, and reach the profound and subtle. May they cultivate that which leads to the attainment of the field of *dhāraṇī*. Through the practice of the Four Truths, may they transform the Śrāvakas in accordance with their needs to lead them to understand the essential truth; guide the various Pratyekabuddhas to still the arising of dependent origination; and encourage them with a single mind toward Samyaksaṃbodhi. Desiring to master all phenomena, they should enter the Mahāyāna; understanding entry into the Mahāyāna, they can subdue the realm of Māra, scatter and abandon the knots of doubt, and transcend the afflictions of transgression. Universally knowing the intentions and conducts of the minds of sentient beings, they accumulate supreme eloquence to expound all Dharmas, manifesting whatever is desired in accordance with all vows.
“Excellent, World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Unattached One, Perfectly Enlightened One!
For the sake of the wise and great beings, you have extensively proclaimed and expounded this, so that all bodhisattvas may attain the power of wisdom.”
To subdue one's own arrogance and attain the superior power of the Dharma;
to understand that the central treasury is without anything created;
and to enable the power of giving, being without stinginess regarding all possessions and bestowing gifts without expecting recompense.
They cause them to attain the power of ethical discipline, which equally eliminates all transgressions and surpasses all vows;
they cause them to attain the power of patience, such that in places where they take birth amidst various painful phenomena, they cherish neither body nor life;
they cause them to attain the power of diligence, accumulating the roots of myriad virtues with a will that is ever free from weariness.

They cause them to attain the power of concentration, dwelling in sublime tranquility and mastery of meditative absorption; they cause them to attain the power of wisdom, transcending false views, doubt, and the darkness of ignorance.

They clarify skillful means to deliver sentient beings, clearly understanding how to provide encouragement and support, and fully mastering the five supernormal powers: the boundless divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, the power of spiritual travel, and the recollection of past lives—by means of these, they roam and delight.
Having attained great eloquence, with the meanings of his eloquent phrases being inexhaustible and uninterrupted, he immediately gains dhāraṇī and his resolve becomes free from confusion.
He causes himself to reach the samādhi of the ocean-seal (sāgaramudrā-samādhi) and perfect concentration; progressing toward universal wisdom, his realization is of a single flavor.
He attains the Buddha’s resolute concentration and practices the path of joyful penetration, forever constantly honoring the Honored One without any obstruction.
Having attained concentration of resolve regarding the Dharma, he exerts himself to advance his concentrated mind; having long heard the Dharma, he is entirely without hindrance.
He honors those with resolute concentration, universally causing all to follow the assembly that never regresses.
Having attained concentration of resolve regarding giving, he has no regret or stinginess regarding worldly wealth or the gift of Dharma, and he is fully endowed with the precepts.
Practice mindfulness and tranquil concentration to swiftly attain Buddhahood, keeping it ever-present in the mind without forgetfulness;
with a resolute will, ascend to the heavens and constantly recollect the Tuṣita Heaven and the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood, delighting in the pure and lofty conduct of Bodhisattvas.
At that time, having finished his inquiry, the Dragon King was joyful and delighted; he again offered verses of praise and addressed the World-Honored One:
"O Great Benevolent One, please explain the meaning for this present life: The conduct and virtues in which a Bodhisattva should enter;
The internal nature and resolve that ought to be cultivated; By what path should one exert oneself, and how should one practice?"
Guided by compassion, enter into the practice of pity; with a mind intent on delivering the multitude, maintain the thought of protection and salvation.
Expand the teaching of concentration and wisdom to make them pure; we pray that you will look upon us with sorrowful compassion and preach extensively.
Guiding the multitude to still the mind and sever conceptual thought— The faculties, powers, and bases of spiritual power proceed thus!
Expounding the path of the seven factors of awakening to the assembly, I pray you explain those virtues that should be honored.
Generosity, self-restraint, and the perfection of virtuous conduct; the power of patience practiced universally along with diligence;
and the immeasurable turning of the causes and conditions of wisdom and resolve—how can you cross over those who are deluded? Please explain this to us.
With eloquence and thorough penetration, you exhort the ignorant and the dark; your resolve and conduct are meticulous and ever-pure.
You immediately awaken to all that arises—pray, speak for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
The virtue of joy brings forth gladness; the seven riches of the noble lineage are the supreme practice.
To delight in dwelling in seclusion and cultivating tranquility—this is solely through the compassionate Honored One’s vast teaching of deliverance.
How does one attain the perfection of eloquence and conduct?
By deeply attaining dhāraṇī, one dwells in eternal peace;
by extensively proclaiming the essential teachings without interruption, one hears them and immediately practices them, never forgetting.
Tranquil, pure, and practicing contemplation, with profound awakening and vast wisdom;
his insight is difficult to fathom and his virtue is boundless—how should one who understands such conduct respond as a bodhisattva?
He subdues the power of Māra and wrathful intent, destroying the various heterodox and evil classes;
his heroic virtue is as immovable as a great mountain, and like the bright moon traveling across the sky, he extensively proclaims the Dharma.
The nature of emptiness and non-conceptuality pervades the dawn; one understands that phenomena are like mirages and illusions.
The substance and forms of dreams are reckoned to be entirely non-existent—may the World-Honored One please grant instruction and explain this!
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon King, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! How truly peerless is this;
that you have yourself resolved to bring forth your doubts and inquire of the Tathāgata."

What you have now asked is sustained by your past merit; you have already manifested great compassion as a spiritual friend for the multitude, not wearying of birth and death, nor severing the Three Jewels.

It is for this reason that you, O King, have raised these inquiries. Listen attentively and reflect upon what you hear, for I shall extensively explain the practices to be cultivated by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—the most essential dharma for attaining infinite fruits for both self and others.
Then the Dragon King said: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
"I vow to joyfully seek to hear them and immediately receive and practice them; I shall proclaim them throughout the ten directions, exhorting others to advance therein without weariness.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One replied to the Dragon King:
"There is a single dharma-practice; if a bodhisattva responds to it, they will be fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks and attain all Buddha-dharmas."
What is meant by "one"?
To give rise to the aspiration for the Way and not abandon sentient beings—this is called the single practice that leads to all Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, there are thirty-two matters for attaining the mind of universal wisdom; one should diligently delight in practicing them, maintaining and cultivating them with focused intent.
What are these thirty-two? They are: cultivating the inner nature;

maintaining the supreme and highest resolve; ascending in the practice of great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*); being firm and steadfast in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); aspiring with tireless devotion; giving rise to diligence (*vīrya*); exerting oneself with fierce perseverance; and possessing the power of virtue.
Furthermore, with a leaping and soaring bearing, he remains tranquil and free from vexation; he exercises patience and endurance for the sake of the multitude and draws near to virtuous friends.

He is dedicated to performing Dharma deeds and wields the power of expedient transformation; he provides fully for the practice of patience and delights in the restraint of the precepts. Deceitful thoughts have already vanished, and he has extinguished and severed all hypocrisy and flattery, so that his words and actions correspond.
His resolve remained steadfast even amidst reversals; he was often filled with a sense of shame and felt inward remorse.

Once his mind became harmonious and joyful, his roots of practice reached the stage of true faith. Controlling his thoughts, he attained the merit of upholding the Dharma; his aspirations turned away from minor paths as he delighted in propagating the practices of the Mahāyāna, observing all matters concerning the Triple Gem so that they might never be interrupted.
"O Dragon King! These are called the thirty-two dharmas; by means of these, a bodhisattva should attain the mind of universal wisdom.
Furthermore, O Dragon King!"
There are sixteen matters that advance and increase the universal wisdom (*sarvajñā*) and manifest the grand track of power.
What are the sixteen ways of advancing universal wisdom?

They are: practicing the giving of universal salvation; possessing the precepts without deficiency; responding with patience through the patience of self-discipline; exerting diligence upon the fruits [of practice]; attaining concentration in all activities; and having already perfected wisdom.

His practice of faith is fully perfected; he serves the Tathāgata, dwells in tranquility, and delights in seclusion. He is endowed with the six firm dharmas and possesses the supreme ten wholesome paths of action.
Adorning his body, speech, and mind, his virtues and conduct are complete; he is contented and finds joy in stillness.
Exhorting others through the three modes of physical action, they cultivate supreme meditative concentration so that all virtues may be perfected.
This is called the matter of the sixteen practices; one should manifest auspicious blessings and develop the mind of great wisdom, clearly upholding the Buddha’s world and freely transforming beings.
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!
That mind of universal wisdom eliminates deviant paths by means of twenty-two matters, and through the aspiration for the Mahāyāna, one cultivates universal wisdom."
What are the twenty-two matters? They are:
transcending the conduct of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; having already cast down arrogance; being free from self-conceit; and eliminating deceitful behavior.

Furthermore, one should suppress vulgar and miscellaneous speech, distance oneself from and discard what is contrary to the precepts, uproot the seeds of anger and resentment, evade demonic activities, and eliminate obscurations and hindrances.
By following the teacher’s instructions, one extinguishes and eradicates transgressions; one should reflect upon oneself with earnest compassion and refrain from discussing the faults of others.
One practices by distancing oneself from evil friends and remaining far removed from those who oppose the virtuous.
One abandons that which is contrary to the six perfections and likewise departs from greed and stinginess; there is no precept that is not fulfilled.
Having already cast aside contention and litigation, one leaves behind indolence and attains self-correction amidst delusion.
Abandoning all ignorance, severing that which is unwholesome, and eliminating evil conduct—

this is called the Bodhisattva’s universal wisdom that universally dispels the twenty-two heterodox paths, swiftly responding with skillful means and never again succumbing to indolence or regression.
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!

By means of twenty-two acts of leaping forward, one advances and follows in accordance with practice to attain the mind of universal wisdom (*sarvajñatā-citta*), which is irresistible; thus one subdues and repels all Māras Pāpīyāns, their demonic retinues, and the followers of external paths."

What are these twenty-two? They are: leaping beyond the matters of precepts; leaping beyond meditative concentration; likewise leaping beyond wisdom and transcending the practice of insight; leaping beyond skillful transformations; and likewise transcending great loving-kindness and leaping beyond great compassion.

To state it briefly: they transcend emptiness, signs, vows, self, person, and life-span; they transcend the departure from various views and the arising of causes and conditions; they transcend the mind’s own purity and the reception of the divine awakening; they transcend the consciousness that perceives what is appropriate or inappropriate to see; and they transcend the practice of the great adamantine firmness.
"O Dragon King! This is called the twenty-two methods of leaping practiced by Bodhisattvas that lead to the attainment of the mind of universal wisdom (*sarvajñā-citta*).
All Māras, as well as their hosts, along with heterodox teachers and outsiders, cannot exercise their power over them; none dare to oppose them, for they completely subdue and repel them."
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!
That mind of universal wisdom is brought forth by relying upon two spheres of practice. What are these two?
To cultivate the spheres of practice as they have been described, and to contemplate the sphere of the path of practice which is the root of all merits—
these are called the two matters of the sphere of universal wisdom (*samantabhadra-caryā*).
Furthermore, there are two matters by which the mind of universal wisdom cannot be destroyed.
What are these two matters? They are:
to harbor no thoughts of superiority or partiality toward sentient beings, and to rescue them from all harmful actions through great compassion.
These are called the two matters by which universal wisdom remains unimpaired.
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!
That mind of universal wisdom possesses two superior dharmas that are unsurpassed; neither the hosts of those in birth-and-death, nor the śrāvakas, nor the pratyekabuddhas can surpass them."
What are these two? They are the adherence to skillful means and the profound practice of wisdom.
These two matters constitute the weighty dharma of universal knowledge.
"Furthermore, there are two things that cause one to abandon the universal wisdom-mind. What are these two? They are:
harboring a mind of doubt and obstruction regarding disparagement, and finding no peace or joy in any worldly pleasures."
These are called the two matters for resting the mind of universal wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two matters for protecting the mind of universal wisdom. What are these two?
Not setting one's aspiration on the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles, but contemplating and beholding the most sublime virtues of the Mahāyāna—
these are called the two matters that protect the mind of universal wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two matters that obstruct the mind of universal wisdom.
What are these two?
A mind constantly inclined toward flattery and an inner nature harboring deceit—
these two matters obstruct the mind of universal wisdom.
"Furthermore, there are two things that do not obstruct universal wisdom. What are these two? They are:
single-mindedly cultivating upright faith and practicing without guile."
These are called the two matters that do not obstruct universal wisdom.
Furthermore, there are four matters that obscure the mind of universal wisdom. What are these four?
To disrupt the true Dharma, to fail to revere Bodhisattvas and wise sages, to be constantly lacking in respect and deference, and to fail to recognize the works of Māra—
these are the four matters that shroud the mind of universal wisdom.
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one remains free from hindrances regarding the mind of universal wisdom (*sarvajñatā-citta*). What are these four?
To protect and uphold the True Dharma; to listen with humility and reverence; to honor Bodhisattvas as if they were the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*); and to constantly recognize the works of Māra."
These are the four matters for the universal wisdom that is unobstructed.
Furthermore, there are five matters that lead to the mind of universal wisdom. What are these five?

Their conduct is free from expectations regarding the outflows of birth and death because they employ the virtue of the precepts; they do not abandon anything because of their great compassion; they regard hatred and love as non-dual because they give away even their own bodies and lives; and they bestow wealth and profit universally because they serve and honor the Dharma.
These are the five matters by which one attains universal wisdom.
Furthermore, there are five matters that advance the mind toward universal wisdom. What are these five?

Associating with virtuous friends, not fearing birth and death, setting one’s will on what is far-reaching rather than the trivial, abandoning untimely thoughts, and seeking the wisdom of all Buddhas—
these are the five matters for advancing the mind of universal wisdom.

"Furthermore, there are five matters within the mind of universal wisdom that surpass the single momentary thought of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. What are these five? They are: surpassing the liberation of the śrāvakas;
surpassing the liberation of the pratyekabuddhas; surpassing the minds of various [limited] knowledges; surpassing all notions of self; and further, surpassing the fetters of habitual tendencies."
These are the five matters that transcend all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, there are five matters by which one finds joy in the mind of universal wisdom (*sarvajñatā-citta*). What are these five?

Delighting in transcending the evil realms, delighting in profound and universal wisdom, delighting in possessing awakened insight, delighting in never being weary of the precepts, and delighting in understanding all practices—
these are the five matters of delight in universal wisdom.
“Furthermore, there are five matters for generating the mind of universal wisdom, whereby one obtains the aid of the five powers and does not sink into birth and death.

What are these five? To be free from anger and resentment by means of the power of patience; to be able to fulfill all vows by means of the power of virtue; to subdue one’s own arrogance by means of the power of wisdom; to apply diligent effort toward extensive learning by means of the power of insight; and to transcend all fears and timidities by means of the power of fearlessness.”
These are the five matters that bring about all supportive powers.
Furthermore, there are five matters by which one abides in the mind of universal wisdom and attains the five purities. What are these five?

They purify by embodying all impure conduct; they purify by means of the roots of the senses that are free from delusion regarding the causes and conditions of those who have fallen; they purify by observing in accordance with all times; they purify by practicing the path of equal skillful means; and they purify by transforming and turning away from all dharmas.
These are the five matters for the universal purification of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are five matters by which one attains the illumination of universal wisdom. What are these five?

To clearly understand desirelessness, to clearly know one's own mind and the minds of others, to be clear regarding the five propositions, to clearly master the practice of wisdom, and to possess the unimpeded eye of clarity—
these are the five matters that bring about the illumination of universal knowledge.
"Furthermore, there are five matters that broaden and universalize the mind of wisdom.
What are these five? They are its five kinds, five roots, five stalks, five branches, five leaves, five flowers, and five fruits."
"What are the five? They are:
daily cultivation of the will, cultivation through practice to purify the internal nature, viewing all people with equanimity, seeking the practice of liberation, and expanding upon skillful means."
These are the five kinds.
What are the five faculties?
Through great compassion, with a root of virtue that never tires, they exhort and advance sentient beings, causing them to escape the Lesser Vehicle and not set their minds on other paths.
These are the five faculties.
What are the five stalks? They are:
understanding skillful means, the perfection of wisdom, guiding and instructing sentient beings, upholding the true Dharma, and viewing joy and anger with equanimity.
These are the five stems.
What are the five branches?
They are the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
These are the five branches. What are the five leaves? They are:

delighting in progress and hearing the precepts; seeking dwelling in empty stillness; constantly aspiring to renunciation; having a mind at peace within the Buddha-seed; and being unimpeded in one’s movements.
These are the five leaves. What are the five flowers? They are:

attaining the perfection of marks and signs because of the accumulation of complete virtues; being fully adorned with the secondary characteristics because of the application of various gifts; possessing the wealth of the seven factors of enlightenment because the mind is free from impurity; achieving manifest eloquence because the Dharma is not obscured; and deeply penetrating dhāraṇī so that what is heard is never forgotten.
These are the five flowers.
What are the five fruits? They are:

attaining the fruit of the precepts, having attained the fruit of deliverance, reaching the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, further attaining the fruit of the bodhisattva’s non-retrogression, and obtaining the fruit of the Buddha-dharma.
These are called the five fruits. "O Dragon King!

These are what are known as the thirty-five matters—the extensive and universal tree of wisdom, the path of precious conduct—for a bodhisattva. One who practices in accordance with them will not find it difficult to attain Buddhahood."
The Buddha told the Dragon King:

"If there are bodhisattvas who wish to receive and uphold these essential phrases of the profound, subtle, clear, and manifest practice of the Tree of Universal Wisdom Mind, they should diligently cultivate the Jewel Tree of Universal Wisdom."
Thus it is, O Dragon King!
I perceive that the merits of all dharmas do not arise except from the profound meaning of this jewel tree;
those who resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path do so entirely because of these essential phrases of the Universal Wisdom Jewel Tree.
For example, O Dragon King!

Just as when one selects and plants the seeds of a tree, and having done so, knows that the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of that tree will eventually become exceedingly lush and flourishing.
Thus it is, O Dragon King!
Those who are able to receive the seed of the mind of universal wisdom have already attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the supreme dharma of wisdom of all Buddhas and noble sages.
Therefore, O Dragon King!

Those who wish to enter the merit of the conduct of universal wisdom and wish to turn the wheel of Dharma should receive, uphold, diligently cultivate, recite, and single-mindedly practice this; they should widely proclaim and expound it for the sake of all beings.
"Thus it is, O Dragon King; you should diligently study this.
When the Buddha spoke these words of Dharma on the Chapter of the Mind of Universal Wisdom, seventy-two thousand among the host of dragons all resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
the dragon king’s crown prince and fourteen thousand ladies-in-waiting all attained the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*).
Five thousand bodhisattvas, by virtue of their past roots of merit, all attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

At that time, Anavatapta, along with other dragon kings and their retinues, used their own supernatural powers to leap up into the void. They raised clouds of incense which suddenly spread everywhere, and a fine rain of harmonious, exquisite fragrances and powdered sandalwood fell upon the Tathāgata and the assembly.

Furthermore, he manifested a wondrous and exquisite canopy of interlaced pearls that completely covered the entire realm of Rājagṛha; all were filled with joy as they sang praises above of the Tathāgata’s supreme accumulation of merit and his immeasurable, holy virtue. Arranged like clouds and the sun, each manifested half their bodies, their radiant patterns filling the void, such that none among the entire assembly failed to see them.
2. Chapter on the Path of Purification (1). Chapter Two: The Path of Purification. Thereupon, the Dragon King again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is most unprecedented."
"So be it, World-Honored One!

It is as the Tathāgata has extensively expounded for the sake of sentient beings—the path of both the mundane and the supramundane, as well as the qualities of the universal wisdom-mind and its practices.
Furthermore, O World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Unattached One, Perfectly Enlightened One!"

I pray that you will expound and explain the conduct of a bodhisattva, the means by which one cultivates purity and becomes wise and sagacious, and how one attains the purity of the Way so as to bring it to its ultimate conclusion—remaining long-term without defilement, without indolence, and without weariness or retreat, until one attains the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, and becomes fully endowed with all the dharmas of the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Anavatapta:
"Excellent, Dragon King!
You have diligently contemplated this practice; I shall now extensively expound the Chapter on the Pure Path of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
Anavatapta said: “Excellent, World-Honored One!
We are fortunate to have received this instruction; we only pray that you will explain it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Dragon King:
"There are eight straight and right paths of bodhisattva practice which you should diligently uphold.
What are these eight?"

The path of the six perfections, the path of benevolent conduct, the attainment of the five supernormal powers, the practice of the four immeasurables, the eightfold noble path, the path of equality toward all sentient beings, the path of the three gates of liberation, and the path of entering into the patience of the Dharma.
Thus it is, O Dragon King!
This is the Bodhisattva’s path of the Eightfold Right Practice.
What is called the Bodhisattva’s path of the Perfections?
Regarding the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), one encourages all acts of charity toward universal wisdom (sarvajñatā). Why is this so?

It is not by merely encouraging the act of giving that universal wisdom is accomplished; rather, when one's practice encourages and assists the roots of virtue (kuśalamūla), it receives the designation "perfection of giving."

Furthermore, by practicing the precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and likewise encouraging and assisting that mind of universal knowledge (sarvajñā-citta), one attains the designation of the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā); this is called the Bodhisattva’s path of the perfections.
"The practitioner of the path of benevolence embraces all sentient beings. Why is this so?

It is because that bodhisattva demonstrates the Dharma-methods; the bodhisattva practices benevolence to embrace all, covering them with the four debts of gratitude while extensively preaching the Dharma, thereby causing sentient beings to compliantly receive the transformation of the precepts."
This is the path of the four debts of gratitude.

Regarding the path of the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*): with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one perceives all Buddha-fields; one sees all sentient beings being born and passing away, and furthermore, one sees the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions surrounded by their disciples—all such things are seen.
Within those Buddha-fields, by means of that divine eye, one should gather and receive whatever is to be gathered.

Furthermore, with their divine ear, they hear the words of all Buddhas and immediately receive and practice them; regarding all sentient beings and various classes of people, they understand them clearly and completely, preaching the Dharma accordingly and attaining the knowledge of past lives, never forgetting the merits performed in previous existences.

Furthermore, possessing the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), one travels through countless Buddha-fields; for those who should be delivered by means of supernormal powers, one immediately exercises them extensively to liberate them—this is the supernormal power that accords with the Way.
"And what is meant by the fourfold path of equality?

O Son of Heaven! When one follows and cultivates the pure Brahmins and all other forms of beings, knowing their mental activities and transforming them according to the day [of their needs], this is compassion, this is loving-kindness, and this is sympathetic joy; it is through establishing them in the Path that they are brought to deliverance."
This is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of the fourfold equanimity.
They universally practice the Eightfold Noble Path; it is that by which Śrāvakas proceed, the cause upon which Pratyekabuddhas rely, and the same is true for the Mahāyāna!
This is called the Noble Eightfold Right Path. What is meant by the path of equanimity toward all sentient beings?

One should not give rise to the thought: "I shall act for this one, but not for that one"; "this may be spoken of, but that should not"; "this person possesses noble virtue, while this other is not a person of merit"; or "this is entirely appropriate, while that is again inappropriate. A Bodhisattva who practices equanimity eliminates all such thoughts; this is called the path of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
"What is called the path of the Bodhisattva’s three gates of liberation?

By means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one severs all false views; by means of signlessness (*animitta*), one eliminates all conceptualizations regarding what is appropriate and inappropriate; and by means of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), one is forever detached from the triple world."
This is called the path of the Bodhisattva’s three gates of liberation.
What is the path for attaining the realization of Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*)?

When a Bodhisattva receives the consecration, he personally awakens to the practice that accords with patience; he becomes one who has received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, regarding the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksambodhicitta*).
This is called the bodhisattva’s path of patience that does not arise.
When a bodhisattva attains these eightfold right paths, they extensively transform and disseminate [the Dharma], guiding others with unimpeded skillful means.
When the Buddha had finished speaking on these eightfold right paths, twenty-four thousand devas, nāgas, and humans all attained realization of the practice of these eight paths.
"Thus it is, O Dragon King!

Because the Bodhisattva applies these eightfold right paths as an equal ointment toward the single refuge, and because they are peerless, there is none who can compare with the Bodhisattva; nor has he any companion, for he walks alone through the triple world. When his mind is tranquil and unified, he cultivates and attains the practice of wisdom. That which should be attained, he has already realized as his own fruit; he clearly penetrates all dharmas as being originally non-existent. This is what is called a Tathāgata!"
This is called the Eightfold Path of the Dragon King.

For the sake of all those various beings who practice in diverse ways, he gives rise to manifold teachings; yet these essential teachings are uniform and of a single direction, taught without expectation, leading toward the teaching of the Unreached.
"How is this path purified? It is said: the path is stainless, because it is free from defilement;
it is dustless, because it is free from passion."
This path is without flaw, for it is fundamentally free from conceptual thought;
this path is without darkness, for its wisdom illuminates all;
this path is without attachment, for it is fundamentally pure.
The Way is eternally without birth, for there is nothing to be extinguished;
the Way is like the eternal non-existence, for it has fundamentally never existed;
the Way is free from taints and impurities, for the three realms are pure.
This Way is quiescent, for it transcends ordinary conduct;
the Way has no destination, for there is no going;
the Way has no point of origin, for there is no coming from anywhere.
The Way is eternally non-abiding, for it transcends all desires;
the Way has no fixed location, for it transcends all views;
the Way is invincible, for it transcends all Māras.
The Way is vast and broadly encompassing, for external paths cannot reach it;
the Way is eternally free from delusion, for those who are arrogant cannot attain it;
the Way admits nothing, for those who do not practice cannot enter it.
This path is extremely distant because it relies on aspiration;
the path is one of eternal detachment because it transcends the conduct of fools;
the path can be realized as a fruit because it is practiced by those who cultivate it.
This path is easy, because one delights in diligent practice;
this path is utterly level, because one abides in right view;
this path is unobstructed, because one cultivates without impairment.
This path is unimpeded because it is the practice of perfect equanimity;
this path is stainless because the three poisons are purified;
this path is pure because it is ultimately free from attachment.
This is called the purity of the bodhisattva path.

If a bodhisattva applies themselves with diligent effort toward this pure path and practices accordingly, they have already become entirely purified within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); they attain the purity of the self-nature (*ātman*) and thereby transcend it as well.
Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is pure, the nature of number is pure;
because the nature of number is pure, the nature of non-number is pure;
because the nature of non-number is pure, one attains the purity of the triple world (*tridhātu*).
Because the three realms are pure, the nature of eye-consciousness is pure;
because eye-consciousness is pure, the nature of mind-consciousness is pure;
because mind-consciousness is pure, one attains the purity of emptiness.
Because emptiness is pure, the nature of all phenomena is pure;
because this purity is functional, all phenomena are equally pure;
and because emptiness is equal to emptiness in its purity, one attains the purity of sentient beings.
Because all things are pure, there is no duality, nor does one cling to duality; because there is no duality and purity, the Path is pure. It is for this reason that it is called the "Pure Path."
He has no manifold thoughts nor does he think of the Path; all thoughts are utterly pure, as if like *nirvāṇa*, and in him they are forever absent—this is called "non-thought.

One should be without that which is to be thought; for one who does not think of the Path, there is also no conscious recollection. That Path is entirely devoid of the activities of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*); speaking from this perspective, it is the Pure Path.
When this Dharma discourse on the Chapter on the Path of Purification was being taught, twenty thousand devas and humans all attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Then Anavatapta again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One?"
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate this purity and proceed toward the Way?
The Holy One replied, "It is so, O Dragon King!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice this mind of pure conduct, they should understand pure conduct and likewise purify their body, speech, and mind.
What is meant by purity of body?
One's own body being already empty, one understands that all bodies are empty;
the body being tranquil, one understands that all bodies are tranquil;
the body being already liberated, one understands that all bodies are liberated.
To understand that the body is indolent and to resolve all bodily indolence;
to understand that the body is like a shadow and to resolve all bodily shadows—
this is called the bodhisattva’s path of purity.

Furthermore, it is said that the body is pure and bodily actions are non-arising. One who contemplates birth and death as non-arising equates birth and death with non-arising; thus, their knowledge of the body also brings clarity to bodily actions.
What is meant by bodily activity?
It refers to the phenomena of going, coming, and arising; the inexhaustible phenomena of arrival; the phenomena of the present manifestation;
and the ultimately inexhaustible phenomena. That which is inexhaustible is called bodily activity.
"Furthermore, the body and dharmas arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; these causes and conditions are empty, without conceptualization, and tranquil, free from thought.
It is thus, O Dragon King!"
This contemplation of the semblance-dharma is called the purity of the body.

Furthermore, if one contemplates that the Tathāgata’s body is untainted (*anāsrava*) and does not fall within the triple world, seeing the body as untainted, suchness, and fundamentally non-existent—because this untainted body does not fall within the triple world.

That untainted body (*anāsrava-kāya*) is able to enter into birth and death; at the limit of the untainted, there is no weariness, relinquishment, or regression. By means of this untainted body, it manifests a form-body (*rūpa-kāya*).
Having manifested in this way, it likewise does not dwell upon the principle of the extinction of the body.

Just as the body of the Tathāgata is pure, so too are the bodies of sentient beings and one's own body pure; they are equal to that which is fundamentally non-existent. This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of purity.
"What is meant by 'verbal speech being pure and appropriate'?
The speech of all, whether wise or foolish, is entirely pure. Why is this so?

Because they employ identical characteristics, ordinary people of inferior capacity become attached to sounds; if their faith is not based on truth, they experience the impermanence of sorrow and joy, delighting in perversions.
One observes that sentient beings have no fundamental basis and are entirely devoid of lust, anger, and the desire for ignorance.

Why is this so? Because all sounds produced by means of various syllables are pure, being free from desire, hatred, and delusion, and likewise devoid of attachment; for this reason, it is called the purity of all speech.
"When one speaks by means of speech, what constitutes that speech?
Is it desire, hatred, and delusion that constitute speech?
Or are the various defilements what constitute speech?"
Speech is unattached; it does not cling to the eye, ear, nose, mouth, body, or mind.
That which is called a "wind-image" is like wind moving and sound emerging: it is only through the convergence of causes and conditions that sound exists.
That which is called "like an echo" means that the speech of both the wise and the foolish is equally like an echo.

That which can be spoken does not abide within, nor does it emerge from without; it cannot be apprehended in between them. It abides in what was originally contemplated and its subsequent practice; that which emerges from speech, along with all contemplations and thoughts, is without abiding and without conceptualization.
"O Dragon King, this is what is meant:
all that the Tathāgata speaks and all the voices of sentient beings are empty and not real; they merely diminish this Dharma! He said:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Is that which the Tathāgata has spoken not true? He replied:
"It is so, O Dragon King! Thus it is with the Tathāgata’s profound discernment."
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata, being one who abides in the truth, understands that all phenomena are neither real nor true.
Furthermore, O Dragon King!

The words spoken by the Tathāgata accord with the sounds of syllables and respond to all the voices of sentient beings; for this reason, sentient beings also turn the wheel of Dharma, yet they do not know that the meaning of the Dharma conforms [to reality]. By means of this retribution, they are made to practice it, and through understanding the various dharmas—the matters of following the Tathāgata’s equality and extinguishing all suffering—they practice in such a manner.

The voices of sentient beings have no fixed abode; though amidst all afflictions, they are ever tranquil. They manifest the desire to speak regarding attachment and non-attachment, and from their voices emerge discourse, discussion, and conversation. That which accords with the Dharma is free from error or contradiction; this is called the purity of a bodhisattva’s speech.
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s mind being pure?
That mind is fundamentally incapable of being defiled. Why is this so?"

Because the mind is fundamentally pure, that which is called the defilement of adventitious desires does not cause the bodhisattva to have any attachment; he understands through skillful means that it is inherently pure from the beginning.

Furthermore, his mental conduct does not select for the roots of virtue; those roots of virtue consist in thoroughly understanding the fundamental nature of the mind. By means of this mental conduct, he extends loving-kindness to all sentient beings, and through clear comprehension, he realizes that they are empty and devoid of self or person. The roots of virtue of his mind assist and encourage him toward the Path, such that he knows the Path as it truly is.
To contemplate in this manner is what is called the purity of mind.
With this pure mind, even when dwelling among those who act with lust, anger, and delusion, one never receives the defilements of desire, wrath, or folly;
and when dwelling among those of virtuous conduct, one does not cling to any impurities.
"This is called the Bodhisattva’s threefold purity of body.
When this Dharma-discourse on the Chapter of Purity was spoken, thirty thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of being born in the place of non-retrogression.
3. Chapter on the Non-Practice of the Path (1). Chapter Three: The Non-Practice of the Path. "Furthermore, O Dragon King!..."

That Bodhisattva, riding upon this pure mind, is born in the realm of desire yet dwells within the realm of form; together with the various devas, he abides amidst the assembly of Brahmās, detailed, tranquil, and serene. In his conduct therein, there is none who can surpass or move him.

Furthermore, this Bodhisattva is able to subdue the various devas through skillful means (*upāya*) and transformative teachings. Or, being born in the realm of form while remaining in the realm of desire, he manifests as having a household and associates himself with all sentient beings in walking, sitting, and rising; yet he does not become weary, nor does he treat sentient beings with arrogance, nor does he disparage himself.

By means of this purity, he brings all meditative concentrations and attainments (*samādhi-samāpatti*) entirely under his own mastery; he does not give rise to anything through the influence of those concentrations.
Why is this so? Because that Bodhisattva must maintain a mind that is pure through the exercise of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"In this way, O Dragon King!
A bodhisattva who understands the practice of purity should cultivate purity and then train in the Path.
Thus it is, O Dragon King!"
The Bodhisattva does not practice by seeking the practice of the Way;
he does not practice by conceiving the practice of the Way through non-practice; nor does he practice with the hope for the practice of the Way, nor does he seek such practice;
he understands the practice of the Way as being non-practice arising from what is produced.
To aspire toward the path is to practice the non-practice of cultivation, whereby cultivation is extinguished and becomes the practice of the path;
likewise, not seeking cultivation is to take it as the practice of the path;
and the non-practice of non-cultivation is the practice of the path.
One does not practice by clinging to renunciation as the practice of the Path;

one does not [cling to] self, person, or life-span; one does not [cling to] the body as impermanent, nor the body as suffering by nature, nor the body as having a self, nor the body as being like a dream, a mirage, a shadow, or an echo;
nor does one [cling to] the body as empty, signless, or wishless.
The body is non-existent; it is the Dharma-body that practices the Way. To state the essential meaning:

the nature of the body and all its sensory faculties do not give rise to the twelve links of dependent origination, nor even to the phenomena of desirelessness from birth through old age and death. There is no counting or non-counting, no duality in practice; there is neither the mundane nor the non-mundane, neither outflow nor non-outflow, neither transgression nor non-transgression. One seeks the practice of the Way through this practice of non-duality.
Furthermore, all phenomena possess the cultivation of non-cultivation; this path is non-cultivation, which is called the cultivation of the cultivation of neither-cultivation-nor-non-cultivation.
Just as space is neither cultivated nor uncultivated, one should cultivate in this way: that this path is non-cultivation;
signless and wishless, it is neither performed as cultivation nor is it non-cultivation—one should cultivate in this manner.
"There is neither attachment nor non-attachment; all phenomena abide nowhere. To diligently practice in this manner is to accord with the training for the Way.

When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke this Dharma discourse on the Chapter of the Path of Training in Purity and Non-Attachment, thirty-two thousand devas and worldlings all attained the forbearance of the joy of the dharma of non-arising.
Furthermore, fifty thousand devas and humans who had not previously resolved their minds upon bodhisattvahood all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Seventy thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of dharmas (dharmakṣānti).
At that time, they all spoke with one voice, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

If there are sons of noble family or daughters of noble family who hear this teaching on the Chapter on the Pure Path of Non-Practice, and having heard it, their minds are not startled or terrified and they do not abandon or retreat from it, they have all received and practiced the intention for the unsurpassed, right, and true path of the Tathāgata, and shall turn the wheel of Dharma turned by all Buddhas.

Furthermore, World-Honored One! These bodhisattvas have all attained the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; they shall distribute this Dharma to immeasurable people and likewise sit upon the lion throne. They shall let out the supreme lion’s roar among the heavens, the world below, and among humanity, just like the roar of the Tathāgata now. They shall subdue and crush the hosts of Māra and the heretics, raise high the banner of the Dharma, and blaze with the radiance of the Dharma. Having struck the thunderous drum of the Dharma, they shall be able to bring down the rain of the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One beheld the assembly of devas, nāgas, and spirits, as well as humans and non-humans, and the fourfold assembly; having heard this most profound teaching, there was none among them who was not filled with joy and satisfaction.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata further expounded this teaching for Anavatapta, speaking in verse:
"The Path is not to be attained through practice; Do not give rise to thoughts of practicing.
Such is the way of the Path: Abandon and depart from the practice of conceptual thought."
One does not seek to cultivate the Path, but sweeps away all divergent thoughts;
that Path has no cultivation at all, pure as the image of the bright moon.
If one gives rise to the thought of cultivation, there is nowhere to cultivate it.
Having transcended the sphere of habitual practice, one attains the supreme path.
This path consists of the thought of non-self, nor does it associate with the habituation of emptiness.
This path is non-dual; it is peaceful, blissful, and unsurpassed.
Life and longevity are likewise; there is no person and no speech.
That Way has no person; it has neither life nor abiding.
Those who practice the Way and wish to dwell in emptiness—
This is far removed from the path of the Sage; it is not the practice of the Way.
The Way is also devoid of conditioning, for it relinquishes the practice of existence.
As it is fundamentally of one single mark, it is eternally empty within emptiness.
The Way has the characteristic of non-arising, And likewise possesses no characteristic of cessation;
Neither arising nor ceasing— All these constitute the practice of the Way.
My voice is like a phantom; One should understand all perceptions in this way.
If one maintains conceptualizations while practicing, from where could the Path arise?
The Path entirely transcends the mundane; therein, there is no habitual practice of the body.
Nor is there the act of extinguishing the body through which one might attain such practice.
This is the abode of the body-faculty; fundamentally, there is nothing to be expounded or expanded.
Therein, no further seeking exists; fundamentally, nothing is unobtainable.
Those who practice this path should regard it as suchness, fundamentally non-existent.
As the fundamental nature is known to be fundamentally non-existent, this is called training in accordance with the Way.
That all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, and that what is realized is like an illusion—
attaining this through understanding and practice is indeed training in accordance with the Way.
If one does not reach the Way, then all that is done remains unestablished;
nothing can stop such activity, for the Buddha-dharma is not attained through such a path.
If it were like the path as practiced, including both practice and non-practice;
What is thus expounded is because one abides in primordial non-being (*mūla-abhāva*).
Those who follow limited paths rely upon inferior vehicles;
this, however, is the unsurpassed path, the very source from which the fundamental vehicle proceeds.
All who cultivate this path attain it without abiding;
this reveals the practice of virtue, whereby one may reach the training for the Way.
The Way is upright and without peril, straight and level.
Diligently practice this path, And forever leave behind all traces of the heterodox.
Just as you, O Dragon King,
Dwell within your own palace;
Without moving from its place, it sends down rain that fills the great ocean;
so too is the Great Being!
He practices the Way according to his conduct.
The Dharma-body is unmoving, yet it can fill the ocean of wisdom.
It is like the Benevolent Dragon King,
who dwells upon the great earth;
As rain falls everywhere in abundance, yet there is no body that is soaked;
such is the virtue of the Bodhisattva!
They practice what has been cultivated in this way.
Employing these methods to fulfill the needs of sentient beings, they remain internally free from attachment,
like the great supernatural transformations of the Dragon King Anavatapta.
The supreme Way and its virtue are thus, Moving and transforming all throughout the ten directions.
Sentient beings have fallen onto deviant paths; Those who fall are attached to views.
For those who abide in this Way, It shall lead them forward to the state of non-action (asaṃskṛta).
Having already abided in this path, the Bodhisattva attains great renown;
he is able to subdue Māra Pāpīyān, as well as those of heterodox and external practices.
He has attained the Way according to Suchness (tathatā), and like the Way, he cannot be moved.
Leaping beyond all mundane dharmas, their conduct is like the lotus flower;
with no folly in the mind of the Way, this conduct is their dwelling place;
thousands of sentient beings they transform and deliver, establishing them in the Way.
By constantly abiding in this path, one attains the five supernormal powers;
with miraculous feet that cause all manner of transformations, one extensively expounds the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
All matters are entirely pure—body, speech, and mind alike.
One should aspire to the path of the noble ones; the nature of persons cannot be known.
Through the practice of patience one becomes unattached, reaching that which is to be attained;
thus one attains the state of a Tathāgata and reveals the path to all sentient beings.
In the ultimate refuge of birth and death, this place is the Tathāgata!
Though one’s departure seems as if reaching somewhere, there is actually nowhere to reach.
Regarding the destination of all sentient beings, one should keep that supreme state in mind.
Studying the supreme path of the Buddha, one sports with illusory dharmas.
Practicing this cultivation of the path is the practice of the Great Way;
such a multitude of virtuous conducts and practices are praised by all Buddhas.
Their virtue is boundless, and can never be exhausted;
those who practice the Way in this manner do not practice nor do they abide.
They find no fault with Māra in that state, for the multitude remains entirely unattached in their conduct.
Those who follow this path neither arise nor cease.
Having attained mastery over their mental conduct, they possess dhāraṇī and vast eloquence;
through generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, they advance ever further like the great ocean.
With defilement of body and speech gone, the mind is pure and pristine;
when stains are eliminated and forever absent, one who practices this path attains the heights of wisdom and reaches the profound and subtle through their conduct.
With wisdom that is difficult to shake and free from attachment, those who maintain and practice this Way—
whether they be the Most Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past, the future,
or likewise the present— they have attained the Way to which the world turns.
Having already escaped all hardships, they have encountered this world that is so difficult to find;
they shall forever be children of the Buddhas—those who hear this Dharma.
How joyful are all sentient beings who, having attained what is most excellent, hear this Dharma!
One should truly serve the Tathāgata, who delights in this sutra.
Those who understand this path are able to sever all emotional attachments;
inheriting his virtue and possessing the various marks, they become generals of the three realms.
The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Extensive Manifestation of the Great Way Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Extensive Manifestation of the Great Way Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.

Chapter Four: Inviting the Tathāgata (Part Two) At that time, Anavatapta, together with his own assembly and retinue, prostrated before the World-Honored One, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We humbly entreat the Celestial Honored One to deign to turn his divine radiance toward us and proceed to the Great Lake of Anavatapta for the duration of three months. We are resolved to joyfully provide offerings to the Holy Honored One, as well as to the Bodhisattvas who have perfected their supernatural powers and the foremost disciples!"
We humbly entreat you to have compassion for us and grant our request, accepting our invitation. Why is this?
How could we, who serve as attendants to the Truly Perfectly Awakened One, ever be worthy of responding to the protocols of a Tathāgata?
I hope to receive the sublime teaching of tranquility; one should make offerings solely with this Dharma.
I pray that I may again hear such teachings as these so that I may always remain joyful; this is precisely how one should serve the Triple Gem!
At that time, the World-Honored One did not accept his request.
He petitioned again:
"In the second month?"
"The Tathāgata will not do so;
[the king asked,] 'May I request one month?
The World-Honored One would not permit it."
"Would you please accept [this offering] for half a month?
The World-Honored One accepted it by remaining silent.

Thereupon, the Dragon King, together with his retinue and generals, saw that the Honored One had accepted the invitation; filled with joy and gladness, a virtuous mind arose within him. He circumambulated the Buddha three times, raised clouds and lightning, and sent down a fine rain that pervaded the entire world. In an instant, he returned and ascended into his palace.
At that time, when Anuttarada attained his seat in the Hall of Righteousness, he immediately summoned his five hundred eldest sons, whose names were:

Shanaya (Good Tusk), Shandi (Good Giving), Shanya (Good Intention), Shanming (Good Clarity), Nengmie (Able to Extinguish), Jixiang (Tranquil Mark), Gandong (Moving), Dawei (Great Majesty), Ganwei (Sweet Majesty), Ganquan (Sweet Authority), Gande (Sweet Virtue), Pucheng (Universal Renown), Weiying (Majestic Valor), Chimi (Holding Honey), Renli (Power of Patience), and Xingxiang (Acting Auspiciously).
These and others, numbering five hundred eldest sons, had already planted the roots for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment in past lives.
The King addressed them, saying: "Furthermore, my sons!

I have now invited the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas and all his disciples, for the duration of half a month. Out of great compassion and profound pity, the World-Honored One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has graciously accepted our invitation."
"You all should unify your minds and exhort one another extensively; show increased reverence for the World-Honored One, the Truly Realized One, the Tathāgata!

Diligently contemplate impermanence, and each of you should remain in tranquility. With humility, respect, and solemnity, wait upon the Tathāgata. You must abandon lustful thoughts, desires, and the pleasures of dragons' play; eliminate greed, anger, and malice; and detach yourselves from desire and from forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile sensations."

Why is this so? Because the World-Honored One is free from desire and is composed and at ease; he is benevolent, refined, discerning, compliant, and tranquil. He is fully endowed with all virtues and surrounded by an entourage of attendants; his immeasurable deportment is entirely sustained by the true and essential precepts of all Buddhas.
For this reason, none of you shall enter the palace for half a month; you must eliminate thoughts of lust, anger, and delusion.

Furthermore, because the Tathāgata will proclaim the Dharma, there will surely be bodhisattvas from other regions endowed with supernatural powers, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, Lokapālas, and the Sudhāvāsa devas, who will all assemble here. You must diligently apply your minds and extensively provide exquisite offerings, adorning and beautifying [the hall] with care so that you do not grow lax midway. This shall cause the members of the assembly to behold the transformation with great joy; this is the true way to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

At that time, after Anavatapta had finished giving his instructions, he immediately created for the Tathāgata, within the Anavatapta Lake at the foot of the Snowy Mountains, a flawless and pure seat of lapis lazuli for the sake of the World-Honored One. It was seven hundred yojanas in length and breadth, most extraordinary and wondrous. Around its perimeter were arranged eighty-four thousand trees made of various precious gems, adorned with a multitude of rare jewels and exquisite ornaments; they were lush and radiant, emitting a brilliant light of a hundred colors from their midst and a beautiful fragrance.

Between the trees, he miraculously manifested eighty-four thousand pavilions made of the seven treasures; their manifold precious radiance was exquisite and peerless. He arranged a hundred thousand ornate canopies of interlaced jewels, from which hung strands of wondrous, rare red pearls.

In each of the halls there were lion thrones; all eighty-four thousand were exceedingly high and broad, spread with priceless, exquisite, and variegated woolen rugs, and provided with couches and seats of precious materials, adorned with latticework embellished by various jewels.

In each hall were two thousand dragons and two thousand court ladies, their complexions exquisite and their beauty immeasurable; their countenances were like blooming flowers and their mouths exhaled fragrant incense. They held various flowers, powdered incense, and unguents, and performed various dances while chanting the virtues of the Buddha to gladden the assembly. Above in the void, they manifested great jeweled canopies extending for a thousand *yojanas*, completely covering the assembly with marvelous gems and colorful carvings. Having performed this transformation, he and his retinue respectfully joined their palms, knelt toward the Buddha, and addressed the Honored One from afar, praising him with verses according to their request:

Wisdom vast and universal, reaching everywhere without obstruction; Supreme Wisdom, with the greatest power, you manifest divine light."
O Great Benevolent One, whose mind acts with wisdom and understanding!
You should observe the various classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions;

foremost in delivering the masses through the practice of compassionate exultation, may you and your assembly be granted this supreme attainment at this very moment.

The Brahma-voice is pure like a thunderclap; with the mournful cries of phoenixes and the gait of a lion, Possessing wondrous sounds that delight all lands, may the hearts of the multitude look forward with joy as you grant them your timely regard.

Sentient beings are exceedingly numerous and universally thirst for you; The Ten-Powered One maintains his power with majesty and no pride.
Great Benevolent One, your virtue is lofty, courageous and resolute; O Sage, by your very nature, you have deigned to ascend and travel here.
Fully endowed with shame and auspiciousness, his virtue is supreme; how could he not rescue and nurture all beings throughout the infinite?
Teacher and friend without peer, he accords with the hearts of the multitude; transforming hundreds of millions of dragons, he gives rise to great compassion.
Majestic and fierce in the world, universally compassionate and saving, you who have mastered all practices according to your will;

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the time for Anavatapta’s invitation had arrived, addressed the bhikṣus:

They said to one another: "The Honored One has gone to the abode of King Atapa; he will surely initiate the transformation of the Dharma and expound the profound and infinite mysteries. The Buddha’s holy majesty and divine brilliance were immeasurable; his faculties were tranquil and settled, and his movements were composed and serene. At that time, the Holy One arrived at the foot of the Snowy Mountains and stayed on its southern side. He then addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:

Then Anavatapta addressed the palace ladies, the crown prince, and his retinue, consoling them, saying:

When a bodhisattva relies upon and accords with the non-existence of causes and conditions, and—free from the extremes of dualistic views—knows both existence and non-existence, they perceive all phenomena as such. Relying on and attached to causes and conditions, they do not see any phenomenon that does not arise from conditions.
They form this thought: "That which relies upon causes and conditions has no reliance upon conditions; it does not rely upon Māra."
Regarding those conditions upon which it depends: they do not say "I am," nor do they say "mine.
Furthermore, within those conditions there is no self and nothing belonging to a self; the conditions have no master, nor is there any grasping or maintaining.
"By understanding how arising occurs through its dependent conditions, one can swiftly and easily attain the mindfulness of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*). What are these four?

Rely on the ultimate meaning and not on the letter; rely on wisdom and practice and not on discursive consciousness; rely on sūtras that accord with the meaning and not on mere conceptual proliferation; rely on the Dharma and not on the person."
"What is meant by 'meaning' (artha)?
What is wisdom (prajñā)?
And what is it to conform to meaning?"
What is meant by mindfulness of the Dharma?
Its meaning is the meaning of emptiness;
it is the non-acceptance of false views and the meaning of signlessness.
One does not cling to the meaning of mindfulness, consciousness, or wishlessness; one does not cling to the meaning of the non-existence of the triple world, nor to numerical categories.

Furthermore, as for "meaning": there is no duality between phenomena and non-phenomena; sounds are unattainable; thoughts are without conceptualization; and there is no dwelling in the locus of dharmas. Because there is no person, life, vitality, speech, or sound—these are all false and non-existent.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning [of the Dharma]: the meaning of the Dharma is the meaning of desirelessness.
What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s pursuit of the meaning of the Dharma?
It is the meaning of being without eye and form, ear and sound, nose and fragrance, tongue and flavor, body and tangibles, and mind and mental phenomena.
The meaning of the non-arising of form, and the meaning of the non-cessation of form;
the meaning of not being [bound by] feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor the meaning of the arising or cessation of the activity of consciousness;
likewise, the meaning of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, and the meaning of the non-arising and non-cessation of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
There is no sense of "self," nor is there the sense of attachment to the view of self;
there is no sense of "person," nor is there the sense of entering through attachment to the view of person;

there is no attachment to the sense of a Buddha-body existing within entry, nor is there the sense of entering through attachment to the names and letters of the Dharma, nor is there the sense of entering through calculating and conceptualizing assemblies.
Furthermore, there is no attachment to the meaning of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
To penetrate thoroughly the meaning of all phenomena—this is what is called the Bodhisattva’s engagement with the Dharma and its meaning.
To follow this meaning without ever regressing is what is called "meaning.
What is meant by "wisdom"?
It is said:
The wisdom of the non-arising of suffering;
the wisdom of non-attention toward its origination;
and the wisdom of the total exhaustion of cessation.
The Way consists of the wisdom of non-aspiration.
It is the wisdom that does not disparage the illusory phenomena of the aggregates, nor the various natures and the nature of dharmas;

it is the wisdom that perceives all sensory objects as empty; it is the wisdom that understands and enters into all dharmas, clearly comprehending sentient beings, and possessing the wisdom of fully developed faculties and unforgotten mindfulness.
He is without thought regarding all states of mental stillness or non-stillness;
he is equanimous toward all states of abandonment, whether wholesome or unwholesome;
and he establishes wisdom through the physical and mental faculties of the bases of psychic power.
Furthermore, there is the wisdom that discerns the lightness and heaviness of the sense faculties;
the wisdom that awakens to all phenomena through the factors of enlightenment;
and the wisdom that has already subdued and harmonized the powers.

The Way consists of the wisdom of the countless, the wisdom of extinction and tranquility, the wisdom of observing distinct phenomena, the wisdom of non-arising at the beginning, the wisdom of non-arrival from the future, and the wisdom of non-abiding in the middle;
it is the wisdom of the body as a reflection, speech as an echo, and mental phenomena as an illusion—this is called the Bodhisattva’s penetrating wisdom.
"And what is meant by a sutra that leads to the goal?

It is that which, arising from these causes and conditions, brings about the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of old age and death, and the realization of non-self; it illuminates the absence of self, person, and life-soul, and provides a profound understanding of all phenomena."
If both the Tathāgata and the self are not the true dharma, yet they are so regarding the three gates of liberation.

Being equal toward the three periods of time in seeking the three kinds of non-attachment—namely, seeing that all dharmas are entirely without arising—and when one views and realizes this, one attains equal cessation, departs from worldly dispositions, and possesses the wisdom of a bodhisattva. Through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one has no doubt regarding any mental conceptions; one should enter into such practice, which is called "conformity to the meaning.
There is nowhere to go and no place from which to come; nirvāṇa is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and has no going or coming—this is called "conformity to the meaning."
"What is meant by 'in accordance with the Dharma' (yathā-dharma)?

Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is eternally abiding. This is called the Tathāgata's suchness (tathatā), which is fundamentally non-existent and without increase or decrease; it is the non-dual, non-differentiated reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). This is termed 'in accordance with the Dharma.'"
Not disparaging the retribution for conduct and the dharma of non-retribution for conduct—this is called being in accordance with the Dharma.
Those of the Mahāyāna proceed by means of the six pāramitās;
those of the Pratyekabuddhayāna attain liberation through dependent origination.
The vehicle of the śrāvakas attains liberation by relying on sound; this is called being in accordance with the Dharma.
Through giving one brings about great merit;
through precepts one attains rebirth in heaven.
Extensive learning and great wisdom;
concentration of thought leading to liberation—this is called being in accordance with the Dharma.

To follow conduct without cultivation, which gives rise to existence and birth-and-death, yet to reach the ultimate purity of conduct and establish oneself in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—this is what is meant by being in accordance with the Dharma.
The foolish rely on the power of desire;
the wise rely on the power of wisdom—this is called being in accordance with the Dharma.
All phenomena are entirely based upon the nature of reality (dharmatā).
"Thus it is, O Dragon King!

That which arises dependent upon causes and conditions should attain mindfulness of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*). Relying upon causes and conditions, one does not rely on the annihilation of existence or non-existence. This is called:
seeing that which arises through causes and conditions is to see all phenomena."
Those who see the Dharma see the Tathāgata!
Why is this? It is because of causes and conditions.
"O Dragon King!
Arising is non-arising; phenomena and non-phenomena are equal, and there is no attachment to them.
Furthermore, as for the Tathāgata..."
It also arises from the conditions of non-attachment, yet there is no arising; dharmas are unattainable. He who awakens to these dharmas is the Tathāgata!
With the eye of wisdom, he perceives their arising from conditions;
that which is perceived by the eye of wisdom is the nature of all dharmas.
One who sees all phenomena is the Tathāgata!
This is what is meant:
he who sees dependent origination sees the Dharma; he who sees the Dharma sees the Tathāgata!
"Furthermore, O Dragon King, the Tathāgata perceives the Dharma through the Dharma. In this way,
if one practices according to this Dharma so as to attain liberation, this is called the bodhisattva’s practice free from desire."
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!

The Bodhisattva free from desire does not cultivate the habits of desire; he delights in the noble ones and abandons those who are not noble.
