He diligently admires and protects the lineage of the noble ones, extensively unifies all wisdom to serve as a guardian for the Dharma, and cultivates extensive learning with a resolve to never forget."

He does not abandon the aggregate of morality; his aggregate of wisdom is unshakable, his aggregate of concentration is immovable, and he attains firm and stable abiding in the aggregate of insight. Because he has attained liberation through the vision of wisdom, his aggregate of liberation through the vision of wisdom is steadfast and difficult to overturn.

"Furthermore, O Dragon King! A Bodhisattva free from desire attains the meaning of the immeasurable true Dharma of the Buddhas and is also endowed with the essential wisdom of countless Buddhas. Furthermore, he realizes the inexhaustible eloquence of all Buddhas and attains the supernormal powers of immeasurable Buddhas. Consequently, he achieves the skillful liberations of countless Buddhas, universally enters into the conduct of immeasurable sentient beings, and travels through countless Buddha-lands. Thereby, he beholds hundreds of thousands of Tathāgatas, and by this cause, he hears countless Dharmas; he attains countless meanings and reaches countless wisdoms, understanding countless practices and delivering countless multitudes."
"Thus it is, O Dragon King!
A bodhisattva free from desire should always be pure, exhausting all defilements so that his virtue is immeasurable; he is autonomous within the three realms and remains unattached."
Why is this so? Because it arises spontaneously from the mind without desire.
There are three things that arise from the mind.
What are these three?
They arise from desire, they arise from craving, and they also arise from clinging.
Furthermore, there are three other modes of arising:
One contemplates arising, and again contemplates arising; one further contemplates the sphere of activity and observes that the mind has no fixed location.
Furthermore, there are three births:
cessation, tranquility, and single-mindedness; through understanding these contemplations, one practices in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are three births:
being endowed with virtue and harmonized by benevolence constitutes tranquility, which arises from diligent practice.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
From straightforwardness in conduct, one is free from flattery, being kind, gentle, and patient.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
being free from hesitation and doubt; being compliant with the wholesome and not coarse; and having contentment in will and being easy to support.
Furthermore, there are three things:
they arise from emptiness, are moreover without perception, and likewise proceed from wishlessness.
Furthermore, there are three things:

All phenomena produced by the mind are impermanent; they arise from that mind. All phenomena are suffering, and this too arises from the mind. All phenomena are selfless, and these likewise arise from the mind.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
that all phenomena arise from the mind as impermanent, that all phenomena are without self, and that cessation and the unconditioned likewise arise from the mind.
All originate from the mind.
"Just so, O Dragon King!
The equanimity of a bodhisattva also arises from the mind; that is to say: "
They do not abandon the mind of universal wisdom because they practice equality toward all through great loving-kindness;
they do not abandon sentient beings because of their great compassion;
and they do not weary of birth and death because of their great sympathetic joy.
They are equanimous toward joy and anger because of their great protection;
they practice the gift of wisdom without expecting recompense;
and they are fully endowed with the virtues and meanings of the various precepts and trainings.

Internally exempting oneself from fault and not discussing the shortcomings of others, one is able to endure the various unwholesome actions of sentient beings, desiring to make their minds as firm as vajra. Gathering the roots of all virtues and manifold merits, one does not spare even body or life to bring about everything [necessary]. Regarding all meditative concentrations and right attainments (*samādhi-samāpatti*), the mind knows no weariness; yet one does not give rise to [attachment] through these attainments. Understanding wisdom through skillful means (*upāya*), one accords with and follows sentient beings, using that truth-wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) to deliver those whose wills seek liberation.

Those who wish to reach the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas should manifest mindfulness of the Buddha and seek all Buddha-dharmas; for they are able to endure suffering in their hearts to widely proclaim the Dharma, thus despising and discarding the offerings and respect of the multitude. Their resolve is complete regarding the various marks [of a Buddha], and they never weary of practicing virtuous conduct; they are filled with wisdom and are extensively diligent in much learning.
By associating with virtuous friends, one encounters spiritual benefactors;
by employing humility and respect, one attains conduct worthy of humility;
by subduing arrogance, one achieves the subduing of arrogance.
Because his resolve and conduct are complete, he fulfills the practice of the mind’s intent;
because he employs no flattery, he is free from the deceitful;
because his words and actions correspond, he is without guile.
Because they cultivate sincerity and faith, they abide in truthful speech;
because they are free from all forms of deception, they eliminate false words;
and because they give rise to sincerity and faith, they subdue their minds within that faith.
Thus it is, O Dragon King!
When a bodhisattva gives rise to such a mind, this is called being without desire.
Furthermore, O Dragon King!
For a bodhisattva who is free from desire, Māra cannot find any opportunity or advantage. Why is this?
Because that bodhisattva corresponds to the infinite and does not practice finite dharmas.
What is meant by these "limited dharmas"?
Desire, anger, and delusion—all of these have limits; because the Bodhisattva does not become attached to them therein, this is called the "unlimited."
The vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are limited; however, for a bodhisattva who abides in the mind of universal wisdom, Māra can never find an opportunity to exploit their limitations.
Where there is mindfulness or the absence of mindfulness, such conceptualizations are limited; the bodhisattva responds by being free from all such thoughts.
For such a bodhisattva, Māra cannot find an opportunity to gain entry.
"Thus it is, O Dragon King!
There are two demonic deeds that a bodhisattva should deeply recognize and should also distance themselves from."
What are the two things?
To lack a heart of reverence toward one’s teachers and friends, while dwelling in great arrogance and looking down upon others—these are called the two.
Furthermore, there are two demonic deeds:
They abandon the treasury of the Bodhisattva’s six perfections and, with minds turned toward delight, personally practice the dharmas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there are two matters. What are these two?
To desire to exercise expedient means while lacking wisdom, and to associate with sentient beings who are fallen into attachment and fixated on appearances, involves two further matters:
being of little learning and meager intelligence yet considering oneself to have attained wisdom through insight, and despite possessing broad knowledge, remaining conceited within it.
Furthermore, there are two things:
to falsely conceive oneself as noble despite possessing very few virtues, or to cultivate virtuous conduct while delighting in the Hīnayāna.
Again, there are two things:
They do not protect the True Dharma, nor do they deliver sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two other matters:

their minds take no pleasure in associating with various bodhisattvas and those who have attained thorough wisdom; they single-mindedly engage in slandering pure and noble bodhisattvas, and as preceptors of the Dharma, they frequently create obstructions.
Furthermore, they obstruct the teacher’s instruction and are full of flattery and sycophancy.
Moreover, there are two demonic activities:
abandoning all roots of virtue while their minds dwell upon what is not virtuous.
Furthermore, there are two things:
though dwelling in seclusion, one harbors thoughts of the three poisons and the mind is constantly agitated; or, when traveling through cities and towns, one has a mind that covets gain.
Furthermore, there are two things:
To preach the profound and essential Dharma to those who are unworthy; to fail to preach it when one ought to do so.
Furthermore, there are two other matters:
failing to recognize the activities of Māra, and becoming distracted in the mental application of the universal wisdom (sarvajñatā).
Thus it is, O Dragon King!
Such are the forms and appearances of these various demonic deeds; yet for a bodhisattva who is free from desire, these never exist.
Furthermore, O Dragon King!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates pure conduct and should be free from desire, they shall attain the sixteen great powers of a bodhisattva; by means of these powers, they shall subdue and harmonize their own will to transform sentient beings.
What are the sixteen powers of a bodhisattva? They are said to be:

the power of aspiration, the power of intention, the power of practice, the power of shame, the power of strength, the power of upholding, the power of wisdom, the power of virtue, the power of eloquence, the power of physical appearance, the power of the body, the power of wealth, the power of mind, the power of spiritual transformations, the power of propagating the Dharma, and the power of subduing all Māras.
The desireless bodhisattva attains these sixteen great powers of a bodhisattva.
"What is meant by the power of resolve of a bodhisattva?
It is thus, O Dragon King!"
That a bodhisattva’s power of resolve (*adhyāśaya-bala*) is able to survey all that has been taught by all Buddhas and to retain it in its entirety—this is called the power of resolve.
That this bodhisattva’s mental intention (*citta*) accords with the practices of all Buddhas and remains unobstructed toward all sentient beings—this is called the power of mind (*citta-bala*).
To be able to penetrate all that is spoken in sounds and to comprehend their various meanings is called the power of practice (*caryā-bala*).
To be free from all unwholesome deeds and to possess the qualities of merit is the power of moral shame (*hrī-bala*).
That all various difficulties do not become non-virtuous actions is the power of strength.
That billions of demonic armies do not dare to confront one is the power of wisdom.
To penetrate and uphold the Dharma, proclaiming and teaching it equally without forgetfulness, is the power of retention.

To remain unattached and unforgetting throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, and to preach all dharmas with unimpeded and uninterrupted understanding—this is the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna-bala*).
That Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings, upon approaching the Bodhisattva, become dimmed and lose their luster—this is the power of physical excellence (*abhirūpa-bala*).
That whatever aspirations one conceives through the "Jewel Head" (*ratna-śīrṣa*) are fulfilled immediately according to one's intent—this is the power of wealth (*bhoga-bala*).
To stand alone as the most honored among all non-Buddhists is the power of the body.
To be able to unify the minds of sentient beings, to know their thoughts, and to transform them through compliant conduct is the power of the mind.
When sentient beings are to be delivered through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he manifests miraculous transformations so that the multitude may behold them; this is the power of supernormal ability.

If the Dharma he teaches is heard by the multitude without interruption, such that they receive it, practice accordingly, and thereby eliminate suffering until its exhaustion, this is the power of the sublime Dharma (*dharmādhiṣṭhāna*).

If, at the time of entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one is able to receive the Buddha’s instructions and practice the dharmas of the worthy and noble ones, this is the subduing of Māra’s power.
This is called the sixteenth great power of a bodhisattva.
“If there are practitioners who aspire to and desire these sixteen powers, they should cultivate desirelessness (*an-iccha*).
For example, O Dragon King!

Just as all rivers flow toward and merge into the great ocean, so too do all the practices of the Path and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) ultimately converge in desirelessness.”
Furthermore, O Dragon King!
Just as all medicinal herbs and trees depend upon the earth, so too do all wholesome dharmas arise from desirelessness (*an-iccha*).

For example, O Dragon King, just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King is cherished by sentient beings, so too is a Bodhisattva who possesses desirelessness beloved by devas, nāgas, ghosts, and the people of the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse for Anavatapta and his sons:
“Those who desire wisdom as Bodhisattvas And vow to attain the Buddha-way,
Should distance themselves from defiled dharmas And always diligently practice desirelessness.”
Wisely understanding the law of dependent origination, one does not rely on the limits of views;
seeing phenomena through dependent origination, there is no phenomenon that exists without conditions.
That which arises through conditions is non-arising; this is not something produced by nature.
Wholesome conditions are likewise empty; knowing emptiness, one has no desire.
Clinging to conditions yet being signless, liberated from vows, tranquil and again tranquil;
serene as one who appears like a great fool, the Māras cannot discern his dwelling place.
Seeing that phenomena are without attachment and conditions, therein there is no self;
since they possess neither a self nor a person, one who knows this is free from desire.
Without a master, there is nothing to guard; there is nothing to acquire, nor anything to relinquish.
Fundamentally liberated, there is neither grasping nor rejecting; Free from desire, one always understands the Dharma.
Contemplating its meaning, one does not engage in ornamentation; In the practice of wisdom, one is always detached from consciousness.
Clearly understanding the sūtras that accord with the truth, One relies on the Dharma and not on persons.
The meaning of emptiness is the Buddha-dharma, as well as liberation from the signless and the wishless;
not relying on the construction of views or thoughts—this meaning is desirelessness.
In the Dharma there is no duality, and sound cannot be apprehended.
Abiding in the Dharma is difficult to disturb; one who is without desire for human affairs is without desire for the Dharma.
Being without desire for the self through the meaning of the Dharma, the eyes do not listen to forms and the ears do not hear sounds;
the nose and mouth are detached from fragrances and flavors, and the body and mind have no further contact with phenomena.
One does not give rise to deportment based on form, nor is one separated from sensation or perception;
there is also no consciousness abiding in a self—one who realizes this accords with the meaning of the Dharma.
There is no abiding in the meaning of the three realms, nor is there any meaning of a "self."
The World-Honored One has no form-body; he teaches the meaning of the Dharma that is beyond words.
Counting and reckoning are not the true meaning; the essential point is not attained through giving.
It is not through precepts, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom—the World-Honored One is selfless.
All phenomena are understood as being without intrinsic meaning; wisdom is said to be the essential core of these phenomena.
Where meaning is eternally non-meaning, desirelessness is the Buddha-dharma.
Through the wisdom that realizes non-arising, one understands suffering; there is neither arising nor cessation.
Neither arising nor ceasing—thus should one respectfully practice.
The five sounds are understood to be like illusions; know them to be such as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Realizing that the internal is like an empty village, one understands this to be desirelessness.
Knowing the ultimate destination of phenomena, one clearly understands the dispositions of sentient beings;
by letting go of thoughts, one brings the mind to rest, and through desirelessness, one attains this wisdom.
With the cessation of mental activity, there is no duality; the supernormal powers arise as the mind becomes light and soars.
Possessing power yet free from pride, with the faculties knowing contentment;
awakened through concentration and liberation by means of wisdom, clearly understanding the Eightfold Noble Path;
observing the practice of cessation with insight, one understands the ultimate destination of the Dharma.
This Dharma has no arising; it has not yet arrived in the future.
There is no dharma abiding in the present; do not seek to know it thus!
The body-form lacks solidity; speech is empty, like an echo.
The mind-illusion is like the wind; for one free from desire, it is thus!
Knowing the Sūtra that accords with the meaning, one thoroughly understands dependent origination;
when fundamental ignorance and birth-and-death are extinguished, freedom from desire is the meaning of wisdom.
Without self, person, life, or lifespan, one understands what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma;
having been liberated from the three gates, that which is taught is emptiness and non-attachment.
Seeing neither arising nor cessation, one cultivates wisdom as an analogy for conventional practice;
not born from mind or thought, this practice is awakened through desirelessness.
The nature of phenomena remains eternally as it is, whether a Buddha appears or passes into parinirvāṇa.
Without duality of awakening and non-awakening, one who has no desire knows this Dharma.
Its accumulation is like the limit of reality; that accumulation comprises all dharmas.
The accumulation of emptiness and the limit of persons—one who has no desire penetrates this wisdom.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) always abides; awakening arises and then passes into extinction.
Not recognizing these two, one is free from desire; such is the nature of phenomena!
Without being afflicted by the wholesome or the unwholesome, one knows that phenomena are devoid of karmic retribution.
The Buddha-dharma does not come from another; it comes from the perfection of practice.
By being detached from awakening through causes and conditions, one transcends the conduct of the śrāvakas through sound.
Generosity leads to great wealth; through that vision and precepts, one is born in heaven.
Through extensive learning one attains wisdom; guarding the mind, one transforms sentient beings.
The Most Holy One guards the mind in all things; such is the Dharma of desirelessness!
With power one constantly turns away from all desires; with wisdom, one’s resolve remains fixed on the Dharma.
Equanimously contemplating all these phenomena, one finds that the nature of phenomena is eternally ungraspable.
Consciousness and wisdom arise through causes and conditions, thereby bringing about the four bases of spiritual power.
Knowing both meaning and phenomena, one accords with the meaning and realizes desirelessness.
Contemplating those conditions, one sees the Dharma; through the Dharma, one sees the World-Honored One.
Equal to the dharma of arising and ceasing, one realizes the Honored One’s Dharma free from desire.
In the traces of causes and conditions there is nothing to be attained; in the sounds of the Dharma there are no words.
This Dharma attains primordial non-existence; this Sage is called the Tathāgata!
Through wisdom one perceives dependent origination, seeing neither a dharma nor the absence of seeing;
with clear wisdom one fully understands dependent origination—this is called seeing the World-Honored One!
He seeks the practice of desirelessness, delighting in the nature of all the noble sages;
not abandoning the Dharma-nature even when it is disparaged, he protects the lineage of the noble ones.
Constantly guarding the Buddha’s true Dharma, he hears without desire and never forgets.
Not abandoning the root of ethical discipline, one attains concentration that is difficult to shake.
With wisdom that knows the body is immovable, one dwells eternally in the body of liberation;
and through the vision of the wisdom of liberation, one always abides in desirelessness.
Understanding all the Buddha-dharmas and the immeasurable paths of the sages;
having attained the divine powers of a Buddha, they are proficient in all practices.
Knowing the mental dispositions and conducts of beings, they suddenly travel through all lands.
They behold all the Tathāgatas and receive the teachings they proclaim;
hearing them, they maintain and understand their meaning, and reveal it to immeasurable people;
they know those billions of practices, and their resolve is directed toward the infinite.
Countless ones shall attain mastery, subduing the mind and entering into merit;
by taming the will so that it is free from desire, they shall never again transmigrate in this world.
Once the mind is liberated from the aggregates (*skandhas*), they thoroughly understand the place of their arising and ceasing.
Contemplating cessation as non-existence, that which is practiced thereby ceases to be.
The nature of sound is the range of the mind; without flattery, one is always upright.
Without guile, disciplined, benevolent, and virtuous—such is the virtue of one free from desire!
By liberation from emptiness, perception, and aspiration, one understands suffering and knows birth and death;
the selfless Dharma is eternally quiescent, and one acts according to the mind free from desire.
Universally knowing the equality of all with loving-kindness, one rescues sentient beings through compassion;
rejoicing without weariness in birth and death, one practices protection without limit.
Bestowing gifts without expectation of reward, one examines oneself and establishes all virtuous deeds.
Endure both the wholesome and the unwholesome, mindful of liberating those sentient beings.
Diligently and vigorously cultivate virtue, reckoning neither body nor life as one's own;
understand the various meditative concentrations in their proper sequence, yet do not become attached to those concentrations.
With wisdom, concentration, and great diligence, they do not fall into the reckoning of numbers;
transforming śrāvakas through the truths, their knowledge does not aim for personal nirvāṇa.
Those who encounter a Buddha’s world without desire possess these various dharmas.
Māra does not know his conduct; he dwells peacefully, having realized this Dharma.
Without desire and without limits, he understands that this is the root of craving.
Free from desire, he is without conceptualization; Māra does not know his whereabouts.
If one conceives of a self and its corresponding objects, they will give rise to demonic activities themselves;
yet those who have completely transcended all conditioned phenomena do not perceive such demons.
With a desireless mind and unforgetting resolve, their conduct is always pure.
Free from desire and without fixed intent, practicing with shame and never transgressing;
by hearing of those who are free from desire, one rejoices in wisdom and honors the Tathāgata.
Abiding in accordance with the Dharma, such a person is truly worthy of being called a World-Honored One.
The Bodhisattvas who wish to serve the ten powers of the Buddhas,
upon hearing this practice of desirelessness, should diligently receive and uphold it.
Having heard this desirelessness, they shall joyfully believe and extensively practice it.
He who constantly attains desirelessness will become a Buddha before long.
Desirelessness is that by which the sages proceed; it leads to the most supreme purity.
Through desirelessness one attains Buddhahood, and thereby transforms beings without limit.
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present—
those who have attained all the various marks and signs of excellence—
all do so by virtue of this desirelessness and because they practice this Dharma.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this chapter on the Dharma of Non-Desire, forty-two thousand devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans present in the assembly all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment;
twelve thousand people attained the patience of non-arising, and eight thousand others attained the patience of compliance;
thirty-two thousand sons of gods, spirits, and nāgas were freed from dust and defilement, and all gave birth to the Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, eight thousand people practiced the path of detachment, and eight thousand bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows without remainder.

At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a brilliant light pervaded the ten directions. Beneath the Snowy Mountains, within the Anavatapta Lake, there appeared all around things never before seen or heard: wondrous flowers of radiant splendor reached up to the knees. Within the waters of that lake, extraordinary and exquisite lotuses grew everywhere, as large as chariot wheels, emitting beautiful fragrances; these flowers were of countless hundreds of thousands of varieties, all brought about by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, and manifested as offerings for this Dharma to gladden the mind of the Dragon King Anavatapta.
The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Broad Path Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Second;
The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Broad Path Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Third.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Attaining the Dharma through Faith (Part Three). Chapter Six: Attaining the Dharma through Faith.

At that time, the Dragon King Anavatapta was filled with great joy; furthermore, the five hundred dragon princes, who had long since resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, heard this teaching of the Buddha and immediately all attained the *anulomikī-dharmakṣānti* (patience in accordance with the Dharma). With immeasurable hearts of delight, each wishing to make offerings, they immediately presented decorated jeweled canopies to the Tathāgata, offering them up to the World-Honored One.
At the same time, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Holy Teacher, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!
You have appeared in this world for our sake."
Why is this so? It is because we have been granted the opportunity to hear the "Chapter on the Universal Path to Faith.

Having heard this, our minds are free from weariness and we do not retreat; nor do we feel alarm or fear. As we hear it, our resolve deepens, and we apply ourselves with single-minded devotion to practice. We take delight in hearing such a Dharma as this, never growing weary.
"Furthermore, O Tathāgata,
please explain how a bodhisattva may encounter the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones. The Tathāgata replied:
“Virtuous sirs, listen attentively with diligent mindfulness; I shall explain this in detail.
The princes replied, “We truly desire to hear it;
those noble beings will receive the instruction of the World-Honored One.”
The Tathāgata told him:
"Venerable one, it is through the arising of faith that one encounters a Buddha.
What is meant by 'faith'? "
Faith means that a true practitioner cultivates all the dharmas of clarity, taking their observance as primary.
What are these dharmas of clarity?
It is said:
One should practice in accordance with the root of virtue without departing from it; one should cultivate the pursuit of joy in the worthy and aspire to follow the assembly of sages;

with a diligent mind, one should establish faith and resolve without weariness or fatigue; and through reflection, one should seek to hear the Dharma, thereby uprooting the aggregates (*skandhas*) and the hindrances (*nīvaraṇas*), while conforming to and practicing the Path.
Having obtained the benefits of the Dharma, they bestow them universally upon the wise; whether toward those who observe the precepts or those who do not, they provide equal aid and support.
Amidst all forms of anger and rage, they always maintain joy; they delight in universal wisdom with minds free from indolence or retreat.
They believe in the Buddha without ceasing, never disrupt the Dharma, and take pleasure in the noble Sangha; their resolve for the Path is unshakable, and they rejoice in what is correct and true.
Furthermore, they distance themselves from arrogance toward others while humbling themselves; they constantly maintain a mind of equanimity, remaining unattached in all circumstances.
Ultimately, they would sacrifice their very lives rather than commit evil deeds. They cultivate sincerity and integrity so that their words and actions correspond with one another.

Their minds are free from defilement through the transcendence of attachment, and their conduct of body, speech, and mind accords with the transformation of the Sages. Thus, they clearly understand all matters and attain...
For the sake of purification, one’s conduct should be pure through contentment and freedom from greed; understanding how to enter the illusion of wisdom, one seeks the faculty of insight.
Relying on and following the seven riches, one cultivates mindfulness and sincerity; equipped with the faculties and powers, one practices right view.
One receives the instructions of teachers and friends with humility and reverence, remaining settled and easy to support, frequently attending Dharma assemblies, and with a mind...
Without retreating or becoming weary of the suffering of saṃsāra, they demonstrate the virtue of the unconditioned through diligent and energetic application of mind;
seeking to ascend to universal wisdom in order to propagate the transformative teachings of the Way, they resolve to leave the household life within the Dharma of the Tathāgata,
cultivating countless pure and holy Brahma-conducts, and establishing compassion to rescue those sentient beings.
His resolve is set upon returning kindness; whether others repay his grace or not, his heart of equal reception and protection remains free from favoritism or aversion.

He does not think of his own benefit but constantly delights in the respect shown by others. His conduct of patience and self-discipline is fully perfected; he never looks upon evil with ill will nor slanders others behind their backs. His inner nature is tranquil, his aspiration is for a secluded dwelling, and his mind always delights in stillness. Devotedly practicing the Dharma, he avoids contention and disputes, treating his own faults as those of others.

Seeking to fulfill the precepts and gathering the practices of meditative concentration, being diligent and prudent in the Path—this is called the conduct of a worthy one that accords with worldly faith.
To establish faith in this manner is what is meant by "arising in the age of a Buddha."
"Furthermore, worthy ones!
To cultivate faith in the mundane world and not forget it—this is called 'arousing faith and encountering the age of a Buddha.
Furthermore, worthy ones!"
What is meant by mundane faith?
It is that those who possess faith:

believe that all phenomena are empty and thereby depart from false views; believe and know that all phenomena are signless and thereby depart from mental application; and believe and know that all phenomena are entirely wishless and devoid of coming or going.
One should know with faith that all dharmas are without consciousness and without thought; that body, speech, and mind are stilled and tranquil, devoid of consciousness;
one should know with faith that all dharmas are characterized by the departure from desire, and are without self, person, or life-span;
one should know with faith that all dharmas are fundamentally without coming or going, being spontaneous by nature.
One knows with faith that the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena is traceless, just as the primordial state is traceless;
one knows with faith that all phenomena are already spontaneous and equal to the traceless nature of space;
and one knows with faith that all phenomena abide in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
One knows with faith that all phenomena transcend the three periods of time;

one knows with faith that all phenomena, though appearing in the realm of desire and amidst false views, are entirely exhausted therein; one knows with faith that phenomena are without attachment, being free from fundamental ignorance and fundamentally pure;
and one knows with faith that the mind of all phenomena is eternally pure, never giving rise to the defilements of adventitious desires.
One has faith that all dharmas are without anything to be observed;
one has faith that all dharmas protect and equally sever all conditioned activities; one has faith that dharmas are selfless, transcending joy and anger;
and one has faith that all dharmas are without mind and without form, and thus cannot be grasped.
One believes that all phenomena are false, like an empty fist used to entice a small child;
one believes that phenomena are without deception, having neither high nor low, and nothing to be discarded or established;
one believes that all phenomena are hollow, like the trunk of a plantain tree.
Faith in the Dharma is as naturally tranquil as the constant state of stillness;
faith in the Dharma is without deliberation and does not abide in the three realms;
faith in the Dharma is eternally non-existent and has nothing from which it arises.
If one believes that dharmas are empty and equal to the infinite;
if one believes and knows that all dharmas are like nirvāṇa, eternally and naturally quiescent—
thus it is, worthy one!
To give rise to such faith within the conventional world is called creating faith and encountering the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, worthy one,
that which is called having faith and encountering the name of the Buddha-dharma is precisely what is meant by the non-arising of all dharmas.

Why is this? It is because form does not arise, nor is there the non-arising of form; it is the habituation of transformative transformation. It is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; since consciousness has already ceased to arise, there is no arising or transformative habituation through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
There is no arising or turning of the body, no delusion regarding existence or non-existence, and no birth, aging, or death, because existence and non-existence do not arise.
Just as when encountering the age of a Buddha, one does not give rise to birth nor does one give rise to cessation;
furthermore, there is no arising of habituation to non-cessation, nor does one encounter the age of a Buddha through the habituation of a lack of right intention or a lack of volition.
To state it in brief: one does not cultivate the practice of non-arising through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;

nor does one cultivate the practice of the path’s non-arising by means of arising wisdom, nor by extinguishing wisdom, nor by being neither wise nor unwise. This is the practice of non-duality, as if encountering the era of a Buddha.

When the "Chapter on Encountering the Buddha through Faith" was being taught, the five hundred princes of the Dragon King Anavatapta all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thereupon, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"Having given rise to faith and encountered the Buddha’s world, One practices the non-arising [of phenomena]."
Those who have no inclination toward faith do not encounter the era of a Buddha.
Cultivating faith is called supreme, for it leads to the pure Dharma;
when one's conduct is sincere, there will be a corresponding retribution, and one shall not deviate from what has been cultivated.
Trusting in and associating with the various noble ones, diligently following them and always paying them respect;
with a mind free from indolence or retreat—this is the practice of faith.
Diligently practicing the hearing of the Dharma teachings, one cannot be moved by the aggregates (skandhas) or the hindrances (nīvaranas).
Attaining the Way through faith, one reaches the stage of gentleness and compliance.
With the wealth acquired through the Dharma, one distributes it widely to provide universal relief;
whether toward those who guard the precepts or those who violate them, one practices faith and bestows gifts equally.
Able to gladden those who are angry, with a mind for the Way that never tires;
diligently seeking the Mahāyāna Dharma, possessing faith and joyfully inclining toward the assembly;
forever free from great arrogance, their will always humble and lowly.
Remaining unattached wherever one may be—such is the establishment of the marks of faith!
With a resolute faith that does not spare even the body, one never commits evil deeds;
guarding what is good, one speaks no falsehoods, so that words and actions are always in accord.
With joyful faith transcending the realms, one delights in practice beyond the mind;
with body, speech, and mind purified, one trains in accordance with what the Noble Ones protect.
Possessing faith and inward purity of conduct, one is always led by wisdom.
Knowing the essential foundation of the body, one seeks out and inquires to proclaim what has been heard.
One regards the seven riches with equanimity, attaining strength and the faculties to be complete;
forever distancing oneself from all false views, one’s resolve is always to practice impartial conduct.
With ritual propriety and reverence, his heart is joyful; he serves with respect as if attending to his own teacher.
His mind is long accustomed to piety and deference; contented, he leaves nothing undone.
His mind is always free from discursive thought; his sole aspiration is the Dharma.
For those who feel weary of birth and death, he leads them to show the virtue of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That which one should practice for liberation is simply to constantly seek a joyful mind;
quickly depart from this world and cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) without weariness.
Embracing all sentient beings, one should rescue them without expectation of gain;
one should repay the kindness thus received, seeking it with joyful faith and diligence.
One does not find delight in one's own benefit, nor does one envy the offerings given to others.
Fully endowed with benevolence and patience, free from flattery and upright in character;
practicing faith in accordance with what the eyes behold, he does not speak of others' faults behind their backs;
his faculties are tranquil and his nature peaceful and alert, his mind finding joy in dwelling in seclusion.
His mind is free from agitation; he exerts himself to fulfill acts of kindness.
First following what is harmonious, he avoids contention; internally reflecting, he subdues his own faults.
Diligently seeking the complete observance of the precepts, he devotes himself exclusively to the path of meditative concentration.
Joyful, faithful, and longing for practice—such are the characteristics of the believer!
Those who wish to surpass faith should practice and understand this:
the Dharma that arises is free from contention; it is profound and subtle, as taught by the Buddha.
Sincerity and faith rest upon emptiness; therein, all manifold views are utterly absent.
All phenomena are devoid of conceptualization; do not intentionally dwell apart from various thoughts.
One should eliminate and sever all such thoughts, thereby awakening to and comprehending the matters of the past and the future.
Seeking the Dharma, one should not form attachments, nor abide in body or mind.
Faith is the dharma of desirelessness; it is free from self, person, and life-span.
Through faith, one understands the absence of origin and attains the state of non-duality.
Its essence is fundamentally without accumulation, its substance being void like space;
faith in all dharmas is likewise, and thus it is identical with the dharma-nature.
It transcends the three periods of time, for all dharmas are without outflows.
Regarding the realm of desire and craving, one delights in faith and remains free from grasping and views.
Since all phenomena are without attachment, their root is luminously pure;
adventitious desires cannot obscure it, for the mind dwells nowhere.
All phenomena are invisible, arising through causes and conditions;
constantly observing noble conduct, one does not accept the defects of what one dwells in.
There is no union and no separation; for the liberated, there is no joining together.
To find joy in the dharma of emptiness is what fools are prone to be deluded by.
When the mind is serene and still, no thoughts arise; deceit and falsehood are like the hollow trunk of a plantain tree.
Speech issues forth spontaneously, neither departing nor existing.
All dharmas are non-existent; what is perceived is entirely without substance.
These dharmas are like empty space, with equal conditions beyond numbering.
All dharmas are like nirvāṇa; fundamentally non-existent, they cannot be seen.
Acting with faith and joy, one understands that the body is empty like space.
Whether they be bodhisattvas or ordinary people, those who possess such faith will encounter and serve the Buddhas; wherever they dwell, there shall be no evil.
Not by means of conditioned form does one encounter the age of a Buddha;
Formless and without location, neither coming nor going;
In form there is no arising, no ceasing, and no abiding.
In the future, there is nowhere to go; meeting a Buddha, one extensively expounds [the Dharma].
The five aggregates are also like this: through transformation and habituation, they turn into non-arising.
Meeting a Buddha, one should dare to speak; O wise ones who have reached the state of Bodhisattvas!
Their bodies and all their faculties are likewise practiced in non-arising;
the Buddha arises through non-arising, constantly rescuing those fallen into birth.
Ignorance fundamentally has no arising, and birth-and-death is just like this!
These conditions are, as they are, originally non-existent; it is from the Dharma that the Buddha arises!
There is no arising and no birth; there is no cessation and no abiding.
Therefore, know that there is no location, and even a location cannot be perceived.
This, too, does not arise of itself; it is expounded extensively by the Buddha.
Without aspiration, there is no abiding; this, too, is what the Buddha has turned.
All elements are likewise so; the seed of the Buddha accords with the Dharma.
Such beings as these also arise from non-existence, And are bestowed equally by the Buddha.
For those whose conduct is thus, The arising of the Buddha is like this;
Delighting in faith in this great state, Its limit cannot be measured.
Chapter Seven: Turning the Wheel of Dharma (3). At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the princes and others:
"Furthermore, O worthy ones!"
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the turning of the wheel of Dharma?

It is when one proclaims such teachings as these, skillfully explaining their phrases and meanings, upholding them without forgetfulness, and practicing them accordingly; and for those who have not yet aroused the mind of great compassion, one gives rise to universal wisdom to accord with the aspirations of all beings, preaching and extensively proclaiming them for them; with a will that never tires and never neglects gain or honor, one exhorts others to maintain mindfulness, to act in accordance with the proper time, and to uphold and protect the practice—this is called the bodhisattva’s turning of the wheel of Dharma.
"Furthermore, regarding the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata—this wheel of Dharma, which manifests and enters into virtue, shall now be explained in brief.

It is not turned by means of arising dharmas, nor by means of ceasing dharmas; it is not turned by means of the inferior practices of ordinary worldlings, nor is it turned by means of the dharmas of noble sages."
Furthermore, this wheel of Dharma does not undergo interruption, for it equally severs neither good nor evil; for this reason, it is called the "wheel of non-interruption.
Moreover, this wheel of Dharma arises through causes and conditions; it turns without arising and without origination; for this reason, it is called the "wheel of non-origination."

Furthermore, this Wheel of Dharma does not turn or follow along with the various sensory faculties—such as eye and form, ear and sound, nose and fragrance, tongue and flavor, body and touch, or mind and mental phenomena. For this reason, it is a non-dual wheel; if there were duality, it would not be the Wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, this wheel of Dharma turns without being attached to the past, the future, or the present; it is the wheel of non-attachment.
Moreover, this wheel of Dharma does not turn through the view of a self, nor does it turn by abiding in [the notions of] a person, a life-force, or a lifespan; it is the wheel of emptiness.
Furthermore, that wheel of Dharma does not revolve through the perception of formations, ideations, or the cessation of mindfulness; it is the wheel of signlessness (*animitta*).
Furthermore, that wheel of Dharma does not revolve in expectation of the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; it is the wheel of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Furthermore, that wheel of Dharma does not turn by calculating differences among sentient beings; it does not abide in dualistic dharmas, such as "this is the dharma of ordinary people" and "this is the dharma of noble precepts," or "this is the dharma of śrāvakas," "this is the dharma of pratyekabuddhas," "this is the dharma of bodhisattvas," or "this is the dharma of the Buddha. For this reason, it is called the non-differentiated wheel.
Furthermore, this wheel of Dharma does not turn by means of a wheel of Dharma that abides; for this reason, it is a wheel without abiding.
"O worthy ones! This is called the 'Wheel of Dharma'."
It is the wheel of true reality, for it is eternally indestructible;
it is the wheel of essential meaning, for it is equal throughout the three periods of time;
it is the wheel of no location, for it equally transcends all habitual bases of views.
The wheel of solitary stillness, because the consciousness that turns is detached and invisible;
the wheel without a nest, because it does not abide in the five realms of existence;
the wheel of ultimate discernment, because no truths are manifested.
The wheel of practicing faith, because it transforms sentient beings with impartiality and without deception;
the inexhaustible wheel, because characters are non-characters;
the wheel of the dharma-nature, because all phenomena rely upon the dharma-nature.
The wheel of the fundamental accumulation of truth, because there is fundamentally no accumulation;
the wheel of fundamental non-existence, because it is like fundamental non-existence;
the wheel of non-creation, because there is no outflow of conceptual thought.
The wheel of the countless leads to the attainment of the holy;
the wheel of space clearly perceives the internal;
the wheel of non-conception is free from external thoughts.
The wheel of wishlessness is so called because it has neither interior nor exterior;
the wheel of non-apprehensibility is so called because its cultivation transcends all limits.
"Furthermore, O worthy ones!

That Tathāgata turns this wheel of Dharma according to the mental activities of sentient beings; yet whether it is turned or not turned, that cannot be apprehended, for there is no dharma to be relinquished.
At that time, World-Honored One!

When this "Chapter on Turning the Wheel of Dharma" was being spoken, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and all kinds of spirits leaped for joy with uplifted hearts. Emitting light, they praised and extolled this Dharma of the Tathāgata, and with one voice they said:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"

It is extremely rare to encounter; when the Tathāgata manifests and teaches the turning of this wheel of Dharma, those who hear it and practice accordingly accord with the wheel of Dharma. This teaching is called the turning of the wheel of emptiness.
All Buddhas of the past, those yet to come, and all those of the present, all do so by means of this Dharma.
Those who have faith therein have already crossed over; we too, World-Honored One, practice this Dharma.

Acting as a supportive advocate for those sentient beings, one who gives rise to this mind and constantly desires to hear this "Chapter on the Wheel of Dharma" should, upon hearing it, resolve to seek the essential practice of this Path; such a person shall also, before long, attain the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

Thereupon, among the assembly, those who heard this teaching were ten thousand devas and humans who all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, while five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Thereupon the World-Honored One addressed the worthy ones, saying:
"Furthermore, noble sirs!
To protect the True Dharma, to receive and uphold the True Dharma, and to maintain and guard the True Dharma—this is called 'protecting the Dharma'."
Why is this? Because it is eternally without cessation.
One who should practice in this way cannot be surpassed by either gods or worldly people.
Then Aśoka came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If such a true person attains supreme awakening through this Dharma, they will have no delusions regarding that which is fundamentally non-existent."

Furthermore, such noble beings as these shall together provide protection; the reason for their protection is to cause these noble beings to quickly respond to this Mahāyāna, so that they may all, having practiced it, attain the turning of the wheel of Dharma and further bestow the great illumination of the knowledge of phenomena.
Therefore, World-Honored One!

By means of these essential teachings of the Dharma, one should provide correct protection so that they may set forth in the Mahāyāna; and by protecting the Dharma-preacher, one should provide peace, rescue, reverence, and salutation, while listening in accordance with the prohibitions and precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the dragon prince Aśoka, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Aśoka, you true gentleman!"

To provide peace, rescue, and protection for those who have set out in the Great Vehicle as Dharma-preachers is called "protecting the Dharma"; it means to attend to, protect, and uphold the True Dharma for the sake of all such Dharma-preachers.
"Furthermore, Aśoka!
Those who protect the True Dharma obtain ten merits. What are these ten?

They are free from the arrogance that descends from their own roots; they practice reverence and are devoid of flattery. They diligently contemplate and delight in the Dharma, aspiring to study it with devotion, focusing their minds on following the Dharma, and practicing contemplation upon the Dharma. They delight in proclaiming the Dharma and delight in practicing the Dharma, acting in accordance with their aspirations and following what has been taught.
These are the ten practices for protecting the True Dharma.
Furthermore, Aśoka! There are ten other matters of practice through which one attains the protection of the True Dharma.
What are these ten? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, upon hearing of a Dharma-preacher, pays homage from afar to that place;

yearns to receive his teachings and, upon his arrival, treats him with reverence and affection; provides whatever he requires, such as clothing and food and drink; protects him in all matters; approaches him with humility and respect; listens to what he says with compliance and proclaims it to his fellow students; prevents anyone from speaking ill of him; and constantly delights in praising him so that his reputation spreads far and wide.
These are the ten matters by which one attains the protection of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, Aśoka! There are four practices of giving by which one attains the protection of the True Dharma.
What are the four? To provide brushes, ink, and white cloth to the Dharma Master;
and to offer robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine to the assembly.
If one hears the Dharma taught by a Dharma Master and praises it with a heart free from flattery;
and having heard it, upholds it and extensively explains it for others—
these are the four kinds of giving through which one attains the upholding of the True Dharma.
"Furthermore, Aśoka!
There are four kinds of diligence by which one upholds the True Dharma. What are these four?

Seeking the Dharma with diligence, diligently and extensively preaching the Dharma, paying homage to Dharma-preachers, and subduing those who disparage the Dharma and the True Dharma through diligence—
these four forms of diligence enable one to uphold the True Dharma.
At that time, the five hundred princes of Anavatapta, having heard the Buddha speak these words, were filled with immeasurable joy, delight, and gladness. In unison they said:
"What the Tathāgata has spoken is most excellent and peerless; it resolves all our doubts."
Each, with their palaces and their respective retinues, offered everything up to the Buddha as a fitting offering; with hearts of reverent obedience, they spoke again with great earnestness:
"From this day forth, World-Honored One!..."

You should diligently receive this transformation, remaining forever without weariness; until you reach the unconditioned state of the Tathāgata, you should together respectfully accept these essential chapters of the sūtra—this precious Dharma taught by the Buddha—and seek thorough mastery while exhorting one another toward its practice.
This, World-Honored One, is our supreme aspiration:

that after the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa, we, your holy masters, wherever we may be in various kingdoms and cities, shall with one mind make offerings to the śarīra, protecting, honoring, and revering it until its final disappearance.
Thereupon, the Venerable Elder Kāśyapa addressed the princes:
"Furthermore, O Viśākha and the rest!
As you have said, you alone desire to preserve the relics of the Tathāgata’s divine body for the purpose of making offerings."

Your words, O disciples, sever for many sentient beings the root of all virtues; they obscure the bright purity and veil the ultimate transformation of the Path, causing you to give rise to such speech. Why is this so?

Furthermore, if the Tathāgata originally made a vow to leave behind relics as small as mustard seeds for the sake of bestowing great compassion upon all sentient beings, how could one receive them in their entirety and worship them alone?
Those true persons then replied to the worthy Mahākāśyapa: “Indeed, Kāśyapa!
Do not limit the Tathāgata’s profound, boundless, and penetrating wisdom with the limited scope of the knowledge possessed by śrāvakas.”
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata possesses the mind of universal wisdom and all-encompassing vision, and through his supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), he can manifest transformations.

Should he bring such a thought to mind, he can cause the devas, nāgas, and spirits throughout the trichiliocosm to each have their palaces completely established as reliquaries, leading them each to think:
"I alone shall make offerings to the Tathāgata’s relics, and not to the others.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
After the World-Honored One has entered the unconditioned state, one should establish his relics in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
If the merit of the Tathāgata were to place a relic, even as small as a mustard seed, atop the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, it would be able to universally illuminate the entire world-system.
"This is the power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to manifest spiritual transformations and inspire beings.
Chapter Eight: Resolving All Doubts and Difficulties (3). At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said:
"O sons of noble family!..."
"Furthermore, is the Tathāgata one who has entered parinirvāṇa? He replied, "Subhūti!..."
"Where there is arising and birth, there must be cessation. Subhūti said:
"O sons of good family!..."
"Does the Tathāgata have birth?
He replied, "The Tathāgata is as he was originally non-existent; though without birth, he manifests birth."
Subhūti said: "If suchness is fundamentally non-existent, neither arising nor non-arising, is it then entirely without arising? He replied:
"Subhūti, this is because that which is born from the Buddha is as it was originally non-existent and has no birth."
Subhūti said: "If the Buddha is born in this manner, how is his parinirvāṇa? He replied:
“Furthermore, suchness is fundamentally non-existent, yet it gives rise to that which is unborn; the unconditioned parinirvāṇa is likewise fundamentally non-existent. O Subhūti!
That which does not arise yet arises—parinirvāṇa is also like this!”
"In this same way, its cessation is likewise so; it was originally non-existent.

When these words were spoken, a great lotus appeared in the Anavatapta Pond, as large as a chariot wheel, adorned with immeasurable varieties of colors and embellished with famous precious gems. Among all the flowers, there was a great lotus whose color was most radiant and brilliant, appearing wondrously beautiful and rising up uniquely high.
The worthy Ānanda, while at the Great Lake Anavatapta, beheld this transformation; seeing it thus, he immediately addressed the World-Honored One:
"What auspicious omen is this transformation, that its arising of such a stirring effect is so profound?"
The Tathāgata said: "Be patient, Ānanda!
You shall see it for yourself."

Not long after these words were spoken, suddenly from the region below—from the world-system called Ratnavyūha in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī—sixty thousand bodhisattvas together with Mañjuśrī emerged from the earth. They transferred themselves to the realm of Śākyamuni and ascended into the midst of the Great Lake Anavatapta, each appearing upon a magnificent and vast lotus flower seat. The youth Mañjuśrī then took his place upon a high, broad, and resplendent lotus seat.
At that time, the entire assembly beheld this and were struck with astonishment and alarm.
Then Anavatapta, along with the various bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and Lokapālas, arrived at the gathering; the multitude all joined their palms and bowed their heads in reverent salutation.
The youth Sumati withdrew and stood in the void, holding a canopy of interlaced jewels and pearls.

Then Sumati, together with all the bodhisattvas and their lotus seats, also leaped into the air at a great distance from the ground; from above, they rained down unprecedented and most exquisite lotuses as an offering to the Tathāgata!
From within the various flowers, a voice emerged, saying:
"The Tathāgata Ratnaketu inquires after the World-Honored One:
'Are your daily activities immeasurable? Is your physical well-being robust? Are your supernatural powers at peace and harmony?'"
The voice spoke again, saying:
"The youth Mañjuśrī, together with sixty thousand bodhisattvas, has gone to the Sahā world-system!

Having arrived at the deep pool of the Dragon King Anavatapta, he observes its miraculous transformations; furthermore, he is intent on joyfully hearing the Dragon King’s inquiry regarding the adornment of the factors of the path and the essential discourse for entering the Dharma, as he extensively exhorts the words of the Dharma for the sake of the World-Honored One, and thus experiences great joy."
Thereupon, Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī) and the various bodhisattvas descended from the void and all approached the Perfectly Awakened One;
they prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata and stood respectfully before the World-Honored One with joyful and solemn hearts.
At that time, the Celestial Master addressed Ruci, saying:
"Come, youth! For what purpose have you come here together with these bodhisattvas?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, while we were in that world-system called Ratnavyūha, the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, we heard that the Truly Realized One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, exists there.”
Out of compassion for the ten directions, you have expounded this essential teaching.
Having heard this Dharma, we have immediately ascended from that land to travel here to pay homage to the Celestial Teacher!
This is because we have heard the Dharma preached by the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
“How near is it,
World-Honored One?”
“Why have you great-minded ones suddenly arrived here from the world-system of Jewel-Ornament in the Buddha-field of Jewel-Essence?

Mañjuśrī replied, “Even if one like Kāśyapa were to sit in a single state of meditative concentration, exerting the power of his supernatural flight to its utmost and exhausting his entire lifespan within it to pass into parinirvāṇa, he still could not reach that land; for the extent of that realm’s boundaries is so vast!”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"That land is beyond sixty Ganges-sands of buddha-fields from here, even reaching the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī. He asked:
"How long has it been since you arrived here? He replied,
"It has been as long as it has taken for an elder to exhaust all outflows and attain liberation of mind."
Mahākāśyapa said: "It is most unprecedented!
Indeed it is so, O Mañjuśrī!"
"The supreme spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) of these [monks] are such as this. Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"Venerable sir, how long has it been since your outflows were exhausted and your mind was liberated?"
He replied, "In the very moment that his mind shifted.
He spoke again:
“Has the Venerable One understood?
He replied, “I have understood.”
Niu-shou spoke again:
"Who is it that binds the mind and then liberates it? He replied:
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
It is through the untying of mental knots that one attains the vision of wisdom, rather than through liberation from what does not exist. He said:
“Venerable Kāśyapa! How can that unbound mind be liberated? Kāśyapa replied:
"To know that the mind is without bondage is itself liberation.
Kāśyapa said: "Yes, indeed!"
By what kind of mind?
How does one know the mind?
Is it known as something past?
Is it in the future or the present?
That which has passed has ceased; the future has not yet arrived; and the present does not abide. By what kind of mind can one know that mind?
He said: "As for one whose mind has already ceased, Niu-shou (濡首) is precisely without any reckoning of body or mind. He asked:
"Does the wise man know that the mind ceases?
He replied, "The cessation of the mind cannot be known."
He asked: "If one attains the state where the mind is completely extinguished, would they forever lack the attainment of bodily consciousness?
He replied:
“O Great Eloquence! Youthful Mañjuśrī! We are weak and inferior;
how could we possibly respond to such words of supreme eloquence?”
Niu-shou spoke again:
"What do you say, Kāśyapa!
Does an echo possess speech?"
He replied: "No, young man!"
"It arises through causes and conditions!
He said, "Did I not say, 'Venerable Mahākāśyapa!'"?
"Are all sounds like echoes? He replied, "They are."
Niu-shou asked again:
"Can eloquence like an echo be brought forth?
He replied:
"It cannot be brought about.
He spoke again: "It is so."

"O Mahākāśyapa! A bodhisattva possesses the talent of expedient eloquence that is inconceivable and lacks any limit; even if you were to question him from eon to eon, O Elder, the bodhisattva’s inspired eloquence would be difficult to exhaust."
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will further exhort Mañjuśrī to extensively expound the Dharma for this great assembly, so that all those gathered may find peace throughout the long night and all beings everywhere may attain illumination in the essentials of the Dharma."
Thereupon, among the assembly was a great bodhisattva named Jñānakoṭi, who asked Mañjuśrī: "For what reason, young man,
does the Elder Kāśyapa, who is so aged and long-established, speak with such timidity and feeble inferiority?"
"For what reason is he called 'the Elder'?
Niu-shou replied, "He is merely a śrāvaka!"
"Therefore, I did not succeed in my argument. Zhijī replied again,
"Is this not a case of failing to understand how to resolve the aspiration for the Mahāyāna?"
He replied:
"Never! Only through liberation by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle."
He asked: "Furthermore, O Ruci!
For what reason is it called the Vehicle of the Śrāvakas?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Noble son!

The World-Honored One, the Able One (Śākyamuni), in accordance with the various sentient beings, has established the teachings of the Three Vehicles and expounded them through his preaching: namely, the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and the practice of the Mahāyāna."
"Why is this so? It is because these beings harbor much greed and their resolve is weak; therefore, I have spoken only of the three practices!
Zhizhi further said:
"What do you think,
Mañjuśrī? Just as emptiness, perception, and aspiration have no limits at all, for what reason are they limited to three vehicles?"
He said: “Noble son!

These Tathāgatas employ the practice of skillful means; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are without limit. For those who are attached to limits and possess limits, they manifest as having limits, yet ultimately they do not limit the practice that is itself limitless.”
He said: "Furthermore, O Śrutarṣi!
We may now withdraw, so that we shall never again have any association with those sentient beings of inferior resolve."
Mañjuśrī replied: "Sons of good family! Be patient for a moment."
"You shall hear from the Dragon King Anavatapta regarding his wisdom, eloquence,
and immeasurable teachings. The Elder Kāśyapa said to Jñānakośa,
"How is it, O Noble Land!"
“In the Buddha-land of that Tathāgata Ratnottama, how is the Dharma preached? Wisdom Accumulated replied: “There is but a single flavor of the Dharma;

from this one Dharma, the sounds of the meanings of immeasurable Dharmas are produced. It discusses only the Dharma of the non-retrogression of Bodhisattvas and the essential treatises on the profound treasury of all Buddhas. One attains liberation through this alone and not by means of various diversities; relying on universal wisdom, there is ultimate and complete liberation. It constantly expounds the pure discourse of Bodhisattvas, for in that land there is absolutely no conduct of cowardice.”
Then Anavatapta asked Mañjuśrī: "Venerable Mañjuśrī, you have come to pay homage to the Tathāgata!
In what manner do you perceive the Tathāgata?"
"Do you perceive the Tathāgata by means of form?
Or do you perceive the Tathāgata by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness? He replied:
"No. "To speak briefly, do you contemplate form as suffering?
Or do you contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as suffering?"
"Do you contemplate the Tathāgata by means of contemplating the cessation of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Or do you contemplate the Tathāgata by means of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness? He replied:
"No," he replied.
Again he asked:
"How can one perceive the Tathāgata through the marks and signs of the past, future, and present, by means of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, or the wisdom-eye?"
He replied, “No. [The Buddha asked: “How so?”
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
By what characteristics do you perceive the Tathāgata? He replied:
“Nāga King! You should contemplate the Tathāgata as being truly the Tathāgata.
He spoke again:
“Mṛdusa! What is the Tathāgata like? He replied:
“The Tathāgata is the equal of those who have no equal; his equality is invisible because he is without peer, and for this reason he is sublime.
O Dragon King!

The Tathāgata is supremely honored; he is without mate, without peer, incomparable, beyond analogy, without compeer, without equal, without match, without rival, and furthermore, he has no form or characteristics.”
Because it is without image, without form, without shadow, without name, without character, without speech, and without reception.
Thus, O Dragon King, such is the Tathāgata; you should contemplate the Tathāgata in this manner!
Nor does one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, or the wisdom eye. Why is this?
Because the fleshly eye perceives light; yet the Tathāgata is neither darkness nor light, and therefore cannot be perceived by the fleshly eye.
Furthermore, the divine eye possesses the characteristic of being conditioned; since the Tathāgata is equal to and transcends all, abiding nowhere, he cannot be perceived by the divine eye.
Moreover, the wisdom-eye knows that fundamentally there are no marks; likewise, since for the Tathāgata all aggregates are eternally non-existent, he cannot be perceived by the wisdom-eye.
“How is it, Mṛdusa! How do you perceive the Tathāgata as having attained purity?”
He said: “O Dragon King!

If one knows that the mind of eye-consciousness does not arise, and further knows that the mind of form-consciousness has neither arising nor ceasing, and if one practices this contemplation while observing the Tathāgata, it shall be pure.”
At that time, those bodhisattvas who had come from the Buddha-land of Jewel Ornament under the Tathāgata Jewel Splendor were struck by what they had never experienced before, and they all exclaimed:
"How wonderful! How marvelous!"
These sentient beings have most auspiciously encountered the Tathāgata!

Having heard this "Chapter on Resolving Doubts as Questioned by the Dragon King," they rejoice with faith; they are neither terrified nor fearful, nor do they feel any alarm or wonderment. Furthermore, they receive, uphold, recite, and proclaim it. Such noble persons should be situated within the precincts of wisdom.
"World-Honored One, we have not come here in vain, for we have encountered and heard this essential, boundless Semblance Dharma.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, wherever this Dharma reaches—whether in villages, kingdoms, or cities—one should know that the Tathāgata is always present there; he shall never enter parinirvāṇa, his True Dharma shall remain undestroyed, and his transformative teachings shall flourish."
"Why is this so? It is because this Dharma chapter is able to subdue the field of Māra and overcome all non-Buddhists.
At that time, Anavatapta said to Mañjuśrī:
“O Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, excellent practitioner!
For such a bodhisattva, once they have heard this Dharma, it is not difficult to attain Buddhahood; they advance themselves and exhort others, diligently pursuing the Path without weariness.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s cultivation of wholesome conduct?
Mṛgāśirṣa replied: “If it is so, O Dragon King!”
Just as the practice of greed is empty, so too is the practice of giving empty; to understand them equally in this way is called wholesome conduct.

To speak briefly: non-restraint and restraint, harboring anger and patience, laziness and diligence, distracted mind and single-mindedness, and likewise folly and emptiness—wisdom is also empty. To practice these things with such equanimity is what is called wholesome conduct.
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!
Just as lust, anger, and delusion are empty, so too is the absence of lust, anger, and delusion empty;
just as the practice of the three [poisons] is empty, so too is their non-mixture empty."
Regarding those equal practices, these are called wholesome practices.
Furthermore, O Dragon King!
Just as the eighty-four thousand practices are empty, so too is the noble and holy right liberation entirely empty; regarding these equal practices, these are called wholesome practices.
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!
If there is a wise and sagacious one who cultivates the bodhisattva practice—neither practicing nor not practicing, yet not perceiving practice;
having no deluded practice and no conceptualized practice, and moreover no knowing of practice—in such equalized practice, this is called 'skillful practice.'"
The Naga King Anavatapta said to Mañjuśrī: "How is it so, O Youth?"
“Does a bodhisattva practice that which is non-practice? He replied,
“O Dragon King!”

From the first aspiration to set out on the bodhisattva path until reaching the seat of enlightenment, all the merits practiced therein arise from the practice of non-arising, the practice of non-appropriation, the practice of relinquishment without acquisition, and the practice of having no abode;
furthermore, they are the practice of non-attachment, the practice of non-truth, the practice of being without limits, and the practice of being without delusion;

moreover, they are the practice of being without lust, the practice of non-action, the practice of being without distinction, the practice of non-examination, and the practice of being without bottom—this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of non-practice.

If a bodhisattva, through the practice of non-arising, neither acts nor refrains from acting, attains the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without fabrication; and by means of wisdom, becomes liberated—permanently liberated even from liberation itself—without transgressing the two extremes, clearly realizing the primordial limit (mūla-koṭi) yet not taking realization as a goal: when a bodhisattva acts in this way, it is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).
"Such conduct as this is what is called 'virtuous conduct.
When these words were spoken, thirty-four thousand devas, nāgas, spirits, and bodhisattva-practitioners attained the patience regarding the dharma of non-arising.
The Sutra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Broad Path Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Three;
The Sutra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Broad Path Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: On the Forbearance of the Non-Arising of Dharmas (4).
At that time, Anavatapta addressed Mṛdvinīya, saying:
"How is the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas to be attained?"
Mṛdusvara replied:
"To endure without giving rise to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—this is called a bodhisattva attaining the patience of non-arising.
Furthermore, O Dragon King!"
The bodhisattva attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) by viewing sentient beings with equanimity to achieve this patience;
he views those sentient beings as being equal to their very birth,
and views sentient beings with equanimity as being without birth.
To view all sentient beings as equal to the nature of reality (dharmatā);
to view all things as they truly are, yet without viewing them as equal by means of equality—this is called the bodhisattva’s patience of the emptiness of equal vision.

"What is emptiness? It is the eye’s consciousness of forms, the ear’s consciousness of sounds, the nose’s consciousness of odors, the tongue’s consciousness of flavors, the body’s consciousness of tangibles, and the mind’s consciousness of mental phenomena."
Just as the sense-faculties are empty, so too is patience empty, the future patience empty, and the present patience empty; as that patience is empty, so too are sentient beings empty.
What is the use of emptiness?

It is because desire is empty, and hatred, anger, and delusion are empty; as sentient beings are empty, so too are the inversions empty. The arising and ceasing of the defilements of desire are also entirely empty. One who practices wisdom in this manner is called a bodhisattva.
Those who practice the patience of the non-arising of phenomena have already turned toward liberation among the multitudes of sentient beings. Why is this so?
Furthermore, that bodhisattva forms this thought:

"Just as emptiness extends to my defilements and to all sentient beings—being empty and non-existent—if one governs desire in this manner, then that desire is already liberated; it was originally non-existent."

All sentient beings possess such patience regarding desire and mastery over it; because they are liberated from these roots of desire, they abide in a state of quiescence that is nowhere to be found. This is eternally unextinguished, neither liberated nor non-liberated, and there is no one who attains liberation. If one is thus eternally liberated, then for that reason, their dwelling place is spontaneous.
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!
If there is a bodhisattva who practices the patience that accords with reality, he delivers all beings without any weariness. Why is this so?
He perceives that all sentient beings are fundamentally unbound from the very beginning and are inherently liberated.
He forms this thought:

"All these sentient beings are attached to a single desire, whereas the practitioner is unattached and thus liberated in the fundamental Dharma. All sentient beings cling to thoughts of unreal and delusive conceptualization; the Bodhisattva understands this, remaining ultimately and fundamentally unattached, already liberated within the source of the Dharma."
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!

A Bodhisattva who has attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), though not yet having reached the essential sphere of practice of the Buddhas, nevertheless does not abide in the stage of ordinary beings, nor in the stages of those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa). They universally enter all spheres of activity and practice the perfections without weariness. They do not engage in lustful conduct in the sphere of desire, they do not become angry in the sphere of hatred, and they do not remain deluded in the sphere of ignorance.

Because they have no desire for any particular place, they abide in the transcendence of all desires; they govern and maintain various lineages to guide and transform sentient beings, while remaining personally free from the defilement of desire and the attachment to foul conduct."
Regarding the realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha, as well as their natural characteristics, he is free from doubt and does not even conceptualize the locus of their dharmic nature.

He manifests universally within those realms of sentient beings, thoroughly understanding the sphere of consciousness and the spheres of both the Dharma and non-Dharma; he is proficient in entering the sphere of practice and observes with wisdom.

In the realm of practice and the realm of birth and death, he neither undergoes birth and death nor enters into following birth and death; in all places where he dwells, he establishes the roots of virtue and maintains stillness without weariness. He understands that birth and death are like the absence of birth and death, yet he does not seek liberation through the cultivation of the noble ones.
Then Anavatapta said to Mañjuśrī, “If you, the benevolent Mañjuśrī,
