speak thus, that a bodhisattva does not attain liberation through cultivation— that one who understands this training is precisely a bodhisattva who attains liberation through cultivation.”
"What is meant by 'a bodhisattva practicing that which is directed toward liberation'? Mañjuśrī replied,
"Attaining non-retrogression— this is what is meant by a bodhisattva practicing that which is directed toward liberation."
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!

A bodhisattva understands that the presence of mindfulness constitutes non-liberation; therefore, for the sake of all sentient beings who dwell in such recollection, they establish diligent progress and transform it into non-recollection. To speak of a 'self' is likewise non-liberation."
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!
That Bodhisattva, being already free from the notion of self, gives rise to great compassion for the sake of those classes of sentient beings who are bound by attachments, and thereby delivers them."

He perceives that birth-and-death is entirely devoid of birth-and-death; he gives rise to all that is born because they are without birth. Seeing that sentient beings are without birth and are all equal, he manifests the taking of a body for the sake of those sentient beings who rely on attachments. He is eternally without birth and likewise has no end. This is the wisdom by which a bodhisattva should practice toward liberation; yet, wielding skillful means (*upāya*), he returns again and again to birth-and-death. In whatever place he is currently born and takes a body, he saves and transforms the ignorant and dark, guiding them with wisdom so they may escape the suffering of transgression.

Because of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the bodhisattva should be tranquil and incline toward liberation; yet, through skillful means, he returns once more to birth-and-death, giving rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for the sake of all sentient beings.

Through the cultivation of signlessness (*animitta*), the bodhisattva should incline toward liberation; yet, by extending skillful means, he returns to wander through birth-and-death, giving rise to great compassion for the sake of those sentient beings who follow their thoughts.

The Bodhisattva’s cultivation of wishlessness should be directed toward liberation; yet, wielding skillful means, he returns to dwell within birth and death for the sake of those classes of beings who follow their wishes, directing his great compassion toward them and performing transformative practices while remaining in the state of wishless liberation.
“Nāga King!

The Bodhisattva understands and enters into the dharma of non-existence, yet does not abandon sentient beings; he enters into selflessness and the absence of a person or life-span, never forgetting the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). He clearly understands and enters into immeasurable fruits, attaining the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Ultimately, he is tranquil and solitary, yet neither in tranquility nor non-tranquility, nor is there any disorder. He transcends all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) equally; being without mind, thought, or consciousness, he does not violate his original vow. He ascends to the mind of universal wisdom (*sarvajñatā-citta*), equally detached from all discursive thoughts. He skillfully understands the various mental activities of sentient beings, whether they have attained the state of a noble one (*ārya*) or are not yet noble. With diligent vigor, he establishes the true holy Dharma and practices without licentiousness; he fixes his resolve without abandoning it. Whether in tranquility or non-tranquility, he equally delivers all across. Without thought or non-thought, for those who are not yet disciplined, he establishes the adornment and solemn order of the Buddha-land. Transcending the mundane, he moves toward liberation, yet even in liberation, he does not depart from the mundane.
Thus it is, O Dragon King!
By wielding the power of wisdom, there is the meditative concentration of the noble ones; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s cultivation that leads toward liberation.
"It is just as, O Dragon King!"
The practice of the śrāvaka should be directed toward liberation, which is termed "going and returning.
Having accomplished that path, they are unable to advance further, give rise to the unsurpassed [resolve], establish great compassion, and transform sentient beings.
In this way, a bodhisattva should also cultivate liberation so as to be no longer subject to movement; having attained non-retrogression, will they not indeed proceed?
O Dragon King!
One should cultivate practice directed toward liberation; without doubt, one shall surely attain the fruit of the Way.

Furthermore, just as a bodhisattva cultivates the path leading toward liberation while never forgetting the fruit of the śrāvaka stage in order to receive the bodhisattva path—whereas the śrāvaka’s cultivation of the path leading toward liberation is limited—the bodhisattva’s cultivation is forever without limit.

O Dragon King! Suppose there were two commoners on the peak of a steep mountain who wished to throw themselves down. One of them was powerful, courageous, and fierce; he was skilled in expedient means, quick-witted, and well-versed in the principles of past training. He understood all transformations and was proficient in every matter. Having thrown himself from that steep mountain, he suddenly returned and remained upon the mountain peak. Because of his valor, vigor, and penetrating intelligence, his body rose with supreme strength and light, swift agility; through the power of his fortitude and resolve, he ensured that he did not fall, nor did he remain fixed in one place.
Just as a person whose will is timid and whose mind is weak, lacking in skillful means, would be unable to throw himself down from that mountain;
so it is, O Dragon King!

That Bodhisattva, regarding all phenomena within emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, observes them without forming any conceptualizations. Having observed them thus, he is further able, through the power of skillful wisdom, to abide in the mind of universal gnosis for the sake of sentient beings.
Those steep mountains are said to be innumerable;
those whose wisdom is vast, penetrating, and manifest with great power are like Bodhisattvas who practice through the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*).

Those Bodhisattva practitioners who cultivate the wisdom of skillful means neither abide in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is called the Bodhisattva donning the armor of universal wisdom (*sarvajña-varma*).
Just as one who enters the realm of death pulls out sentient beings and causes them to resolve upon the bodhisattva’s Mahāyāna practice,
whereas those who are weak and inferior remain on that mountain and cannot return— this is likened to the śrāvaka who does not enter saṃsāra and thus provides no benefit to sentient beings.
"If it is so, Dragon King!
Those bodhisattvas who hear this 'Chapter on the Essential Practice of the Wisdom of Liberation,' O World-Honored One,
shall all attain firm resolve in the mind set upon supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment, and will swiftly approach the seat of Buddhahood to deliver beings from the three realms."
When this Dharma was being taught, seven thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly attained the stage of non-retrogression. Chapter Ten:

The Essential Dharmas for the Assembly (4). Chapter Ten: The Essential Dharmas for the Assembly. At that time, the prince of the Dragon King Anavatapta, named Kandaka, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Now, World-Honored One! I...”
With a mind free from greed, I take refuge in the Triple Gem, vowing that this sutra may long abide in the world for the sake of protecting the True Dharma.
World-Honored One!

Having resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, I vow to cultivate these practices and joyfully promote their fulfillment. May I realize the root of the mind, clearly understand the root of the Way and the roots of all dharmas, and personally achieve the most supreme enlightenment of Buddhahood, widely proclaiming the transformative teachings of the Way to nourish all sentient beings.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Those bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this chapter on the Dharma of the Pure Great Path, do not believe in it with joy nor practice it, should be known as a class of bodhisattvas who have been bewitched by Māra; they shall not swiftly draw near to the practice of the mind of universal wisdom.

Why is this? From these essential meanings of the World-Honored One’s Dharma-chapter, bodhisattvas are born; they personally attain buddhahood, subdue demons and non-Buddhists, and all the perfectly awakened Buddhas of the past, future, and present arise through this very Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to the prince: "How marvelous!

Since you, O worthy one, understand the fundamental nature of the mind, clearly realize the fundamental nature of the path and all dharmas, and have attained awakening to all dharmas—what is this fundamental nature of the mind by which such realization was attained?"
He said: "As for its root, Subhūti, that root is the root of the mind."
Subhūti asked: "What is the root of the mind? He replied:
"It is rooted in lust, anger, and delusion.
He asked, "What are lust, anger, and delusion rooted in?"
He replied: "It takes mindfulness and non-mindfulness as its foundation. Subhūti said:
“Venerable sir, how is it?
Do lust, anger, and delusion arise and originate from a lack of mindfulness?
He replied:
“Subhūti! The roots of lust, anger, and delusion are fundamentally non-recollection; they do not arise even as non-recollection.
Furthermore, their root is non-arising.”
Furthermore, Subhūti!
As for that which can be spoken of, what is the fundamental nature of this mind?
That which is the fundamental nature of the mind is fundamentally pure; this is called the fundamental nature of the mind.
"As originally pure, he is free from the defilements of lust, anger,
and delusion. He said, "Noble son!"
"If desire arises and gives rise [to further existence], from what does that arise?
And how is it that birth constantly arises without interruption? He replied:
“Subhūti! That which desires to arise does so only as it arises; yet, regarding the fundamental nature of the mind, there is no attachment to arising. Indeed, Subhūti!”
If that mind inherently possessed attachment, it would never attain ultimate purity;
therefore, the mind is fundamentally devoid of attachment.
From this, one knows that desire is also pure.
Subhūti said: "How is it, son of good family!
Do you thoroughly understand desire?"
He said: "Because they arise through causes and conditions, that which lacks causes and conditions does not arise. Indeed, Subhūti!"
"One who cultivates pure mindfulness realizes that desire does not exist. Subhūti asked:
"Furthermore, how is this so?"
“Son of good family!
Should a bodhisattva cultivate pure mindfulness?
He replied:
“Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices all practices within their conduct, this is called a bodhisattva practicing pure conduct. Indeed, Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, dons the great armor of virtue and transforms them until they reach nirvāṇa, yet perceives that sentient beings are fundamentally identical to nirvāṇa—this is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of pure mindfulness.

"O Subhūti! When a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas according to their needs, yet does not follow along with those transformations, this is called a bodhisattva practicing the cultivation of pure mindfulness."
"Indeed, Subhūti! Furthermore, when that bodhisattva pacifies his own desires and stills the desires of sentient beings, this is called a bodhisattva practicing pure conduct.
Moreover, Subhūti!"

As for that bodhisattva, while abiding in pure mindfulness they perceive what is not cultivated, and within the impure they perceive cultivation of purity; this is called a bodhisattva who practices the cultivation of purity.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the prince Kandaka, saying:
"Furthermore, what is it like,
son of noble family?"
"A Bodhisattva perceives purity in that which is not cultivated; how does he perceive pure cultivation of mindfulness in that which is not cultivated?
[The Buddha] said: "Subhūti!..."

To cultivate pure mindfulness means to cultivate the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and fragrances, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects; seeing that none of these are cultivated as dualistic, and that their dharma-nature is non-dual—this is called cultivation.
"Not being attached to the three realms is the dwelling of a bodhisattva; to dwell by means of skillful means (upāya) is what is called the cultivation of mindfulness.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices in this way, they are said to be one who cultivates the practice of pure mindfulness."
Thereupon the World-Honored One praised the Prince, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Just as you, a true gentleman, have spoken with such inspiration, practice purity in this very way!"
This is what constitutes the pure conduct that a bodhisattva should cultivate.

Whatever has been spoken here is entirely through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha. If there are bodhisattvas who practice in this manner, they are indeed those who should give rise to the practice of the Mahāyāna; one should know that such individuals are firm in universal wisdom.
Thereupon, the Prince was moved and addressed the Buddha:
"How is it, World-Honored One?
By what means may a bodhisattva, with a mind free from desire, take refuge in the Buddha?"
He said: "Noble son!

If there is a bodhisattva who thoroughly understands that all phenomena are without self, person, or life-span; that they are without form, without perception, and without the mark of phenomena; and who does not perceive the Tathāgata within the nature of phenomena!"
In this way, a bodhisattva, being free from desire, should take refuge in the Buddha.

Just as the Tathāgata’s Dharma is the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and just as that dharmatā is universally pervasive, one who attains this dharma-nature and thereby knows all phenomena—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva, with a mind free from desire, taking refuge in the Dharma.
That which is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is immeasurable.
One who practices the immeasurable is a śrāvaka.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva perceives the immeasurable as such, and regarding that immeasurability neither conceives of it as measurable nor as dualistic, this is called a bodhisattva taking refuge by means of a mind free from desire.

When these words were spoken, the Prince was moved and attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). The assembly of gods of the form and desire realms, nāgas, and humans—twenty thousand beings in total who heard this Dharma chapter—all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

Chapter Eleven: Receiving the Investiture and Prostrations (Part Four). Chapter Eleven: Receiving the Investiture and Prostrations. At that time, the Dragon King Anavatapta, together with his palace ladies, crown prince, and retinue, surrounded him as they took refuge in the Triple Gem. He offered his entire palace, along with everything belonging to the pond, to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus to serve as a vihāra.
Furthermore, he spoke these words: "Now, O World-Honored One!"
I give rise to this aspiration: from this great pond, may four rivers flow out to fill the four seas.
World-Honored One!

May all living beings—whether dragons, ghosts, humans, birds, or beasts; whether two-legged or four-legged—who drink from these flowing rivers, all resolve their minds toward unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

"For those who have not yet awakened from their past [karmic] tendencies, having drunk this water, they shall bring their practice to fulfillment, swiftly reach the seat of Buddhahood, subdue the hosts of Māra, and overcome all non-Buddhists.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled.

When the Buddhas smile, five-colored light issues from their mouths, radiating with countless, shimmering flames that illuminate the immeasurable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions. This brilliance surpasses the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, and the jewels of the heavens; it eclipses all the celestial lights of the palaces of the Māras, Śakra, and Brahmā, leaving them in darkness.
At that time, there were countless billions of devas who, without exception, felt joy and made vows for holy awakening.

The light penetrated all the great hells, including Avīci; those touched by its brilliance were immediately freed from their manifold sufferings, and all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of enlightenment.
It circled the World-Honored One countless times and suddenly entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, there was a worthy named P’i-chi (in the language of Ch’in:

*pien-ch’i*, meaning "eloquence"), who, upon seeing that radiance, immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt before the Buddha with palms joined in reverence, and spoke in praise of the World-Honored One with these verses:
“His color is immeasurable, bringing joy to all who behold him; the Bull among Men, the supreme and peerless World-Honored One!
Having extinguished the manifold darkness and brought forth great illumination, he wields majestic spiritual power and speaks with a smile.”
Your virtue, praised by a hundred blessings, is perfected in its seven aspects; having attained the light of wisdom, you expound the practice of insight.
As the supreme teacher of the Dharma, you alone are the Dharma King; World-Honored One, for what auspicious omen do you smile now?
Possessing insight into the truth and always delighting in faith, with faculties stilled and tranquil, he is honored by all through his manifold skillful means;
he brings all beings to liberation through profound stillness, for his virtues are infinite and he speaks with a smile.
The Brahma-voice is pure, penetrating, and exceedingly gentle; its tone is elegant and refined like that of a phoenix, surpassing all other music.
All sounds are complete and without deficiency; he smiles and proclaims this teaching for the sake of liberation.
The light of wisdom and liberation accords with the perfection of insight; his conduct is ever pure and he delights in detachment.
Through skillful means he understands all practices and is endowed with universal wisdom; this King of Guides among the noble ones explains the meaning of his smile.
With wisdom and eloquence thoroughly penetrating, your insight is boundless; you manifest immeasurable power and are fully endowed with supernormal faculties.
Having perfected the ten powers, you move all beings universally; Teacher of Gods, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The light from his body shines immeasurably through the profound darkness; the myriad lights of the great trichiliocosm cannot obscure it.
Surpassing the sun, the moon, pearls, and fire, the majestic and holy radiance is without equal.
Your merit is as full as the great ocean; you transform bodhisattvas through the light of wisdom.
With boundless intelligence, you dispel all doubts; for what reason do you manifest this smile?
The Honored One has crossed the three realms without limit; through skillful means, he removes the defilements of sentient beings.
Able to purify the stains of desire until none remain, for whom does your celestial countenance now break into a smile?
The Tathāgata’s movement stirs all beings universally, shaking the devas, nāgas, and various spirits;
I bow my head in homage to the Dharma King, seeking his explanation of the smile’s meaning to resolve the doubts of the multitude.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the elder, the venerable Bhadrika:
"Do you see Anavatapta? It has been adorned with such magnificence for the sake of making offerings to the Tathāgata."
He replied: "Indeed, World-Honored One!"
After a while, he saw him and said:

"This Dragon King has planted the roots of virtue under ninety-six billion Buddhas; now he receives this investiture and honor, just as I was prophesied by the World-Honored One, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, in a former life:"

"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Conduct, Supreme Benefactor of the Multitudes, Unsurpassed Charioteer of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans—Buddha, World-Honored One!"
At that time, the Dragon King, for the sake of the elder’s son—whose name was Piśudana (in the Dan-ben [Chinese] edition; in the Jin translation:
Jingyi, "Pure Intention")—heard me receive the prediction of enlightenment and immediately conceived this aspiration:
"May I, in a future life, obtain an official appointment just like this Brahmin, who has been predicted by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
"At that time, the elder’s son Pure-Mind was none other than this Ānanda Dragon King!

Furthermore, during the Bhadrakalpa, this dragon king shall adorn this pond with various treasures intermingled in such a way that it resembles a celestial palace; he shall offer all of these in service to the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa."
All these Tathāgatas, fully knowing the King’s intention, have all expounded this Chapter on the Pure Dharma; they are all seated here just as they are now.

Furthermore, as in the past, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa likewise sat together upon this lion throne, and the final Tathāgata, Ruci, shall also turn the essential meaning of this Chapter on the Dharma.
The Dragon King Anavatapta shall make offerings to the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa; having heard this Dharma from them, the assemblies of all those Buddhas will be exactly as they are now.

After countless eons following this, he will serve the Tathāgatas and attend upon the many Perfectly Awakened Ones, cultivating pure Brahma-conduct, constantly protecting the True Dharma, and exhorting Bodhisattvas to advance!

Then, after seven hundred incalculable eons have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Anavatapta Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfectly Endowed with All Practices, Unsurpassed Charioteer of Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans—Buddha, World-Honored One!
"In this way, worthy one!
When the Tathāgata Anupadhiśeṣa attains Buddhahood, the people of that land will be entirely free from greed, anger, and delusion; they shall never harm one another nor speak ill of each other."
Why is this so? Because those sentient beings are fully endowed with the resolve and conduct [necessary for it].
Thus it is, worthy one!

The Buddha Anavatapta, the Arhat, the Tathāgata, shall have a lifespan of eight billion years, and his assembly of disciples shall likewise number eight billion. Just as his first assembly was pure, so shall it remain from beginning to end without any deficiency or decline. Throughout hundreds of thousands of such assemblies, there shall be four thousand billion Bodhisattvas who possess eloquence and have received their prediction of enlightenment, all gathered together; furthermore, the number of Bodhisattva practitioners who have resolved to attain awakening shall be incalculable.

"When the Tathāgata Vigatātapas becomes a Buddha, his land will be pure, with the ground made of deep blue lapis lazuli, inlaid with various jewels and adorned with celestial gold; he will construct pavilions and walking paths out of many kinds of luminous pearls."
If the sentient beings of that land conceive the thought of food, a hundred flavors shall immediately appear, and they all attain the five supernormal powers.

As for the dwellings and residences of the people in that country, they enjoy precious jewels, clothing, food and drink, and amusements with complete freedom, exactly as it is in the fourth heaven, Tuṣita.

They have no dualistic thoughts, nor do they harbor any mind of greedy desire or sexual conduct; rather, all sentient beings delight themselves in the joy of the Dharma, and the people of that land are entirely free from the defilement of desire.

If that Tathāgata expounds the Dharma like a spreading rain without any thought of weariness, manifesting countless supernatural transformations to propagate the great edification, proclaiming the scriptural teachings without ever encountering difficulty, and as soon as he is suited to preach the Dharma, sentient beings are immediately delivered.
Why is this so? It is because all their aspirations have reached full maturity.
Furthermore, within this trichiliocosm, the Tathāgata himself brings about transformation through a single Dharma alone, with no external heterodox paths.
Furthermore, whenever the Tathāgata wishes to assemble the multitude, he immediately emits light from his body that illuminates the entire realm; the people of that land then all think:
"The World-Honored One has awakened and is about to expound the transformative Dharma, which is why he radiates this light!"
Each, sustained by the Buddha’s holy supernormal power, flew forth to attend upon the Buddha and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, that Tathāgata never fails to manifest his supernormal powers; suddenly ascending into the air to a height of seven *zhang* from the ground, he took his natural lion throne and extensively expounded the discourse on the Dharma for the great assembly. All those in the land beheld him, as if gazing upon the palaces of the sun and moon when they are at their full and brilliant splendor.

Because sentient beings have planted roots of virtue, they are born in that land. The people of that country behold the World-Honored One’s lion throne suspended in mid-air without any point of attachment; immediately they understand that all dharmas are likewise empty and without attachment.
At that time, all attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
That Tathāgata spoke only of the gateway for entering the adamantine concentration (*vajrasamādhi*), without any mixed discourse concerning *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*.
The reason why only the Vajra-samādhi is expounded is as follows: for example, wherever a vajra strikes, there is nothing it does not penetrate and shatter.
Likewise, the Dharma taught by that Tathāgata is also like a vajra, drilling through and pulverizing all doubts, attachments, and various views.
"In this way, worthy one!

When the Buddha Anavatapta manifests his parinirvāṇa, there shall be a venerable bodhisattva in that world named Dhṛtipraṇidhāna; only after he has been granted the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) will [the Buddha] manifest his parinirvāṇa."

Just as that Buddha was about to pass into extinction, the Bodhisattva Dhṛtipraṇidhāna immediately attained unsurpassed, most correct enlightenment; he then succeeded to the Buddha’s position, being named the Tathāgata Samatulya, the Unattached, the Equanimous Perfectly Enlightened One!
"The number of bodhisattvas possessing supernatural powers and the assembly of senior disciples in that land shall be as great as those of Lake Anavatapta!

At that time, the crown prince of King Anavatapta, named Dangdan Changxin, was filled with reverent joy. He presented to the Tathāgata a precious luminous pearl and a canopy adorned with latticed jewels, and with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha:
"Who, at that time, shall become a Bodhisattva Who Holds His Vows?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the direction of the Prince’s faithful intention, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dhṛtipraṇidhāna, who was destined to succeed the Buddha, is none other than this present Dragon Prince Dantadhara!"
At that time, as the Tathāgata Anavatapta was about to pass into extinction, the Bodhisattva Dhṛtipraṇidhāna immediately ascended the Buddha’s seat;
furthermore, as the Tathāgata Samatulya, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Awakened One, had just attained Buddhahood, he likewise turned this essential core of the Dharma-discourse.

When the Buddha had spoken this "Chapter on the Consecration," forty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The bodhisattvas, Śakras, Brahmās, Lokapālas, devas, nāgas, and spirits who had gathered from the worlds of the ten directions, having heard the Buddha speak this Dharma of consecration, were all filled with joy; their hearts leaped with exultation, and they gave rise to faith and delight. Prostrating themselves with their five limbs to the ground, they each returned to their palaces.
King Anavatapta, surrounded by his princes and retinue, commanded the nāga-elephant king Elapatra, saying:

"For the sake of the Tathāgata, construct a jeweled chariot adorned with latticework and exquisite gems, making it vast, sublime, and boundless; you shall convey him to the Truly and Fully Enlightened One!"
"I shall now receive your instruction.
He immediately manifested for the Tathāgata a carriage made of the seven precious jewels with a jeweled lattice canopy, making it exceedingly high, large, vast, and magnificently adorned.

The World-Honored One, the Bodhisattvas, and all the disciples sat within the carriage. The Nāga King Anavatapta’s prince and his retinue, their hearts filled with reverence, together pulled the carriage by hand from his palace out to the great pond. By the Tathāgata’s divine will, they suddenly ascended Vulture Peak.

12. Chapter on the Entrustment of the Dharma-Treasury (Part Four). Chapter Twelve: The Entrustment of the Dharma-Treasury. Thereupon, when the World-Honored One had arrived at Vulture Peak, he addressed Maitreya, the youth Mañjuśrī, and the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of noble family!
"Since the Dharma-factors (dharmapada) concerning that which Anavatapta asked should be proclaimed and expanded upon again,
so that those who have not yet heard them may hear them," Maitreya and Mañjuśrī both addressed the Buddha:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to speak out of compassion."

At that moment, the World-Honored One immediately radiated light of countless colors; heaven and earth shook six times, and the brilliant radiance shone forth, illuminating the ten directions. The various honored Bodhisattvas from the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, who were fully endowed with supernatural powers, immediately flew through the air upon seeing the light and arrived. They all bowed their heads in prostration and each took a seat.

King Ajātaśatru, the queen, the court ladies, the crown prince, his retinue, the ministers and subjects of the entire kingdom, the elders, the householders, the brahmins, and the scholars—upon seeing this radiance and hearing that the Tathāgata had returned from Anavatapta—each abandoned their affairs and proceeded together to Vulture Peak. Arriving before the World-Honored One, they were filled with solemn reverence; joining their palms in salutation, they paid homage and inquired after the Tathāgata’s well-being, saying:
"Are your blessings immeasurable?"
He then withdrew and sat down again, gazing at the Buddha without weariness.

The radiance of the Tathāgata’s body reached everywhere throughout the infinite worlds; it descended and penetrated all the dark and gloomy places of the great hells, such that there was no being in the hells who was not touched by its light.
Furthermore, from that radiance, a voice issued forth, saying:

"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni has extensively expounded the essential Dharma of the Chapter on the Path of Purity at Lake Anavatapta; he now returns to Vulture Peak to once again manifest his transformation."

Furthermore, his voice reached all the hells; the various classes of sentient beings in the hells of the ten directions were instantly freed from the pains they endured, and they all saw the Buddha and the assembled multitude from afar, whereupon they all lamented in sorrow:
"Alas, World-Honored One!"

We have endured countless sufferings and the bitterness of the hells; we have been scorched and roasted by the six fires surrounding us, subjected to the myriad wounds of sharp blades and the hardships of boiling cauldrons; through these various transformations, we have undergone these manifold agonies for days and months ever more distant.

How excellent it is that these worldly beings have encountered and served the Tathāgata; by receiving the Buddha’s transformation through the Way, they have attained liberation from the three sufferings. Although we ourselves encountered various Buddhas in past lives, we did not receive their Dharma transformation and were thus subjected to manifold pains. By relying on the chapters of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, our various calamities and offenses have been immediately lightened.

At that time, all sentient beings in the hells throughout the ten directions—numbering in the tens of billions—simultaneously conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. Receiving the Buddha’s sacred power from afar, they spoke with one voice, saying:

"All suffering is fundamentally pure; he who realizes this fundamental nature is free from delusion. It is only because we failed to realize this that we have undergone countless sufferings in these various hells. We pray that all may swiftly understand perfect truth."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, the youth Mañjuśrī, and Ānanda, saying:
"O sons of noble family!

You should diligently receive this essential exposition of the sūtra, uphold it, recite it, read it, and propagate it; explain this Dharma extensively for those who study it, so that the fourfold assembly may apply their minds to its dedicated practice—this essential conduct of wisdom which accords with the accumulation of eloquent phrases and meanings."

If sons or daughters of good family should give rise to a joyful mind and turn toward this sutra with delight, one should for their sake explain these profound and deep meanings—the inexhaustible treasury where all paths converge and to which all scriptures return; these are the accumulated essentials of all Buddhas, subtle and immeasurable. Whatever is thus bestowed, one must ensure that every word and phrase is clear and distinct, without addition or subtraction.

Furthermore, if there are noble sons or daughters of good family who, regarding all the merits and various practices performed by the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, have upheld the teachings spoken by those Buddhas, training in each one with single-minded devotion and diligent practice.

Furthermore, if one practices the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; and if one serves these Buddhas along with their assemblies of disciples, providing them with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, incense, flowers, music, and whatever else they may desire;
and if one constructs monasteries and walking paths, honoring and revering them in such an immeasurable way;

When the various World-Honored Ones have entered parinirvāṇa, one might erect stūpas made of the seven treasures for those Tathāgatas and make offerings to each of these Tathāgata stūpas with incense, flowers, music, silken banners, canopies, and by offering burning incense and lamps, as well as hanging various jewels such as the night-shining moon; though such offerings may be extremely numerous and beyond measure, if one were to calculate and sum the merit of these deeds, it would not equal that of a son or daughter of good family who attains even a single hearing of this "Chapter on the Meaning of Resolving All Doubts" from the *Anavatapta Nāgarāja-paripṛcchā*.

Why is this? Because this treasury of Dharma is the most supreme wisdom that gives birth to the essential practices of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; how much more so for those who uphold it, hold the volume and recite it, comprehend its profound subtlety with a mind free from doubt, and further proclaim and disseminate what they have heard—the merits of these acts are immeasurable.
At that time, Maitreya, the youth Mañjuśrī, and the venerable Ānanda together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly unprecedented.
Indeed it is so, World-Honored One!"

Furthermore, because the Tathāgata’s compassion descends upon all and he gives rise to great pity, for the sake of the bodhisattva practitioners of the ten directions—past, future, and present—as well as devas, nāgas, spirits, and all sentient beings, he extensively expounds the meaning of this Dharma, the chapter on the Infinite Purity of the Path.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If sons or daughters of good family, upon hearing this *Anavatapta-nāgarāja-paripṛcchā-vinaya-saṃśaya-sūtra*, do not immediately receive, uphold, delight in practicing, or recite it; nor do they widely disseminate, demonstrate, or study it equally; nor do they give rise to the mind to encourage and assist others in doing so—then one should know that such sons and daughters of good family have provided an opportunity for the various Māras, their retinues, and heterodox outsiders, and will remain constantly caught within the net of entanglements and doubt.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"How excellent are these words!
You exhort all beings to practice this Dharma and cause them to act in accordance with it."
The Tathāgata further said:
"You should propagate and extensively expound this sutra for the fourfold assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas Maitreya and Mañjuśrī, as well as the Venerable Ānanda, all addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will graciously accept and propagate this Dharma.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
what is the name of this sutra?”
"How, then, should one serve? The World-Honored One replied: "O clansman!"

It is titled "The Chapter on the Pure Dharma that Resolves All Doubts as Requested by the Naga King Anavatapta," and is also titled "Extensively Manifesting the Way through the Samādhi of Broad Illumination. You should diligently receive, uphold, and master the essentials of this sutra.
"Furthermore, O clansmen and others!
These factors of the path are the precious guardians of the ocean-deep sutras of all dharmas.

Then Maitreya Bodhisattva, the youth Mañjuśrī, and all the assembled bodhisattvas endowed with supernatural powers, along with Śakra, Brahmā, Lokapālas, devas, nāgas, and spirits, spoke to the Buddha with one voice:
“Excellent, Tathāgata! You have well expounded this Dharma.
We, O World-Honored One!”

In whatever villages, kingdoms, districts, or towns this Dharma is practiced, we shall personally protect and sustain those practitioners, ensuring that those who hear it are not subjected to evil interference;
we ourselves shall also uphold this sutra, causing it to spread everywhere so that it may never be interrupted.
The Buddha praised Maitreya, the youth Mṛdusvara, and the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent, sons of good family!
What you have said to encourage and gladden the bodhisattva practitioners of the future is most truly marvelous!"
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas with supernormal powers who had gathered from the ten directions all attained manifest concentration;
fifty-four thousand devas, nāgas, spirits, and humans all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment;
and five thousand devas and humans attained the Dharma-eye.

The Dragon King Anavatapta, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the youth Mañjuśrī, all the bodhisattvas, and the venerable Ānanda, along with the fourfold assembly and the various devas, nāgas, and diverse spirits—both human and non-human—heard what the Buddha had said and were all filled with joy; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and each withdrew as they pleased.
The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Propagation of the Way Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
